title: Computing Foundations — How Computers Actually Work

lessons.title: Bits and the audacity of counting with two fingers
paragraphs: Welcome. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations, the class where we find out how computers actually work. This is lesson one, and its title is Bits and the audacity of counting with two fingers. Settle in. By the end of this lesson you will know what a bit is, why a machine that can only tell the difference between two things can still count, spell, show photographs, and play music, and you will be able to count to thirty-one on the fingers of one hand. That last part is not a party trick. It is the whole secret, hiding in your own hand.

Let me say plainly what this lesson teaches and why it is worth knowing. Every photograph on your phone, every message you have ever sent, every file for your business, every song and every video, is stored inside a computer as numbers. And every one of those numbers is built out of the smallest possible choice, a choice between two things only. If you understand that one small choice, and how it multiplies, you understand the ground floor of every computer on Earth. Nothing later in this course will make sense without it, and everything later in this course is built on top of it. So we start here, at the bottom, where the ground is solid.

Here is my promise about how I teach. I will never hand you a word without telling you what it means in plain language first. I will never ask you to guess what a good answer looks like. In this room, the worked example is a moral act, because nobody should have to guess what good looks like. When I set you a small problem, I will work one in full, out loud, before you ever have to try. Watch for that. It is coming in this very lesson.
First, let us talk about counting itself, because counting is something you already know how to do, and the computer does it in a stranger and simpler way than you do.

When you count, you use ten symbols. They are the digits zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine. Ten symbols. That system is called decimal, and the word decimal simply means based on ten. It is almost certainly based on ten because you have ten fingers, and human beings learned to count on their fingers long before they learned to write numbers down. There is nothing magic about ten. It is just the number of fingers we happen to have. If we had been born with eight fingers, we would probably count in eights and think it was the most natural thing in the world.

Now here is the audacity in the title of this lesson. A computer counts with two fingers. Not ten. Two. The computer has only two symbols to count with, and they are zero and one. That system is called binary, and the word binary simply means based on two. Everything a computer does, all of it, is done with those two symbols and nothing else. When I first heard that, years ago, I thought it sounded impossible, like trying to write a novel with only two letters. It is not impossible. It is just slower to read and much, much faster to build. By the end of this lesson, you will see why.

The smallest piece of this whole story has a name, and the name is bit. A bit is one single choice between two values, and those two values are zero and one. That is the whole definition, and I want you to hold onto it exactly as I said it. A bit is one single choice between two values, zero and one. The word bit is short for binary digit, which just means one digit in the binary system, the way the number seven is one digit in your ordinary decimal system. One bit, one choice, two possible answers. That does not sound like much, and on its own it is not much. One bit can say off or on. One bit can say no or yes. One bit can say dark or light. But wait until you see what happens when bits travel in groups, because that is where the power is.

Why two? Why would anyone build a machine on such a small choice? The answer is electricity, and it is a practical answer, not a poetic one. Inside a computer, a bit is carried by electricity in a wire, and the machine reads the bit by asking a simple question about that electricity. Is the voltage high, or is the voltage low? Voltage is just the push behind electricity, the pressure that makes it flow. High push, the machine reads a one. Low push, the machine reads a zero. Two states of electricity, two symbols, and the machine never has to guess. Imagine instead that we tried to build a computer on ten levels of voltage, one for each decimal digit. The machine would have to tell the difference between level four and level five in a wire full of noise and heat and tiny imperfections, billions of times every second, and it would get it wrong. With two levels, far apart, there is almost nothing to get wrong. High is high. Low is low. That reliability is the entire reason for binary. Computers count with two fingers because two fingers are almost impossible to misread.

You already own a perfect picture of a bit, and you use it every day. A light switch. A light switch has exactly two states, off and on, and it is never halfway in any way that matters. One switch, two states. That is one bit, sitting on your wall. Now picture the panel in a hallway with four switches in a row. Each switch is off or on, and the row as a whole can be in many combinations. Off off off off. On off off off. Off on off on. Count the combinations and you get sixteen, and we will see in a few minutes exactly why it is sixteen and not some other number. Hold that picture of the switch panel in your mind, because a computer is, at the bottom, an enormous panel of switches, switching faster than anything you have ever seen, and keeping perfect track of every combination.
Now let us learn to count in binary, slowly, with our hands, because your hands are the best teaching tool you own.

In decimal, when you count, you fill up one place and then you carry. You count zero, one, two, all the way to nine in the first place, and when you run out of symbols you write a one in the next place and start again, and that gives you ten. The places in decimal are worth one, then ten, then one hundred, then one thousand. Each place is worth ten times the place before it, because decimal is based on ten.

Binary works in exactly the same way, except each place is worth two times the place before it, because binary is based on two. So the binary places, reading from the right, are worth one, then two, then four, then eight, then sixteen, then thirty-two. Say those place values with me, because you will use them in every lesson that follows. One, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two. Each one is double the last. That doubling is the heartbeat of this entire subject.

Now count with me in binary, and watch how the carrying happens sooner, because we run out of symbols sooner. Zero is written as 0. One is written as 1. Now we have used both of our symbols in the first place, so to say two, we carry. Two is written as 10 in binary. Read that carefully. It is not ten. In binary, the written form 10 means one two and no ones, which is two. Three is written as 11, meaning one two and one one. Four needs a new place, and four is written as 100, meaning one four, no twos, and no ones. Five is written as 101, meaning one four, no twos, and one one. Six is written as 110. Seven is written as 111. Eight is written as 1000. Do you see the pattern? The symbols look like the decimal numbers you know, but they mean something different, because the places are worth different amounts. The written form is just a row of switches. The value depends on what each place is worth.

Here is how you read any binary number, and this is a skill, so we will do it as a worked example, in full, the way I promised. Take the binary number 101, written as the digits one, zero, one. Step one, write out the place values under the digits, from the right. The rightmost digit sits over the ones place. The middle digit sits over the twos place. The leftmost digit sits over the fours place. Step two, multiply each digit by its place value. One times four is four. Zero times two is zero. One times one is one. Step three, add them. Four plus zero plus one is five. So the binary number 101 is five. That is the whole method, and it never changes, no matter how long the binary number gets. Places, multiply, add. Places, multiply, add. If you can do those three steps, you can read any number a computer has ever stored.

Let us do one more together, a bigger one, so the method settles. Take the binary number 1101, the digits one, one, zero, one. The places from the right are one, two, four, and eight. The leftmost one sits over eight, so that is eight. The next one sits over four, so that is four. The zero sits over two, so that is zero. The last one sits over one, so that is one. Eight plus four plus zero plus one is thirteen. The binary number 1101 is thirteen. Good. You have just read a computer number the way the computer means it, and you did it in your head, with no machine to help you. That is doing it, not watching it, and that is how this room works.

Now it is time for your fingers to earn their place in the title of this lesson. This is the guided part, the doing part, so actually do it. Hold up one hand, palm facing you, and look at your five fingers. Here is the idea. Each finger is a switch. A finger held up is a one. A finger folded down is a zero. Your hand is now a row of 5 bits, and like any row of bits, it can hold a number.

We need to agree on what each finger is worth, and we use the place values you already learned. Let us say your thumb, on the right of your raised hand as you look at it, is worth one. The next finger is worth two. The middle finger is worth four. The next finger is worth eight. And the little finger, on the far end, is worth sixteen. One, two, four, eight, sixteen, one for each finger. The number your hand is holding is simply the total of the fingers that are up.

Try it with me, step by step. Start with a fist. Every finger down, every bit zero. Your hand is holding zero. Now raise only your thumb. One finger up, worth one. Your hand is holding one. Fold the thumb down and raise the finger worth two. Your hand is holding two. Now raise the thumb as well. Two plus one. Your hand is holding three. Fold both down and raise only the middle finger, the one worth four. Your hand is holding four. Raise the thumb too. Four plus one is five, and notice what your hand is showing. Middle finger and thumb up, the rest down. That is the binary number 101 spread out on your own hand, the same 101 we worked out a moment ago. You are not imagining a computer. You are being one, slowly, at human speed.

Keep going on your own for a moment, because your hand will teach you faster than my voice can. Show me seven. That should be the fingers worth four, two, and one, all up together, because four plus two plus one is seven. Show me ten. That is the finger worth eight and the finger worth two, because eight plus two is ten. Show me thirteen. Eight plus four plus one, so the eight finger, the four finger, and the thumb. If your hand found thirteen, you have understood binary counting completely, and everything else in this lesson is just that same idea getting bigger.

Now here is the question that makes people sit up. What is the biggest number one hand can hold? Raise all five fingers. Sixteen plus eight plus four plus two plus one. Add them. Sixteen and eight is twenty-four, and four is twenty-eight, and two is thirty, and one is thirty-one. One hand, five fingers, and the biggest number it can hold is 31. And how many different numbers can that hand hold, counting zero? It can hold every number from zero up to thirty-one, and that is 32 different values in total. Five fingers, thirty-two values. Remember that pair of numbers, because a pattern is about to show itself, and the pattern is the most important arithmetic in computing.

The pattern is this. Every time you add one more bit, the number of possible values doubles. Watch it happen. With 1 bit, you have two values, zero and one, and that is 2 values. With 2 bits, each value of the first bit can pair with each value of the second, and you get 4 values, zero through three. With 3 bits, you get 8 values. With 4 bits, you get 16 values. With 5 bits, your hand, you get 32 values. With 6 bits, 64 values. The count of values is two multiplied by itself once for each bit. Teachers call that a power of two, and all that phrase means is two doubled over and over. So if X is the number of bits, then the number of values doubles X times. Hold onto that sentence in plain words. More bits, double the values, every single time. That is why a handful of extra bits is never a small thing. Eight bits is not a little more than seven bits. It is exactly twice as much room.

Now use both hands. Ten fingers, ten bits. The values double ten times, and the total is 1024 different values, the numbers from zero up to 1023. Two hands, and you can already count past a thousand. A person counting on ten ordinary decimal fingers can show ten things. A person counting in binary on the same ten fingers can show one thousand and twenty-four different numbers. That is the audacity of counting with two fingers. The two-symbol system looks poorer and turns out richer, because combinations multiply. Every bit you add doubles the world the machine can describe.

This doubling is also why computers feel like they leap instead of grow. When an engineer adds bits to a machine, she does not add a little room. She doubles the room, and then doubles it again. Small changes in the number of bits make enormous changes in what can be represented. Keep that in your pocket for the whole course. Whenever a number in computing looks strangely large or strangely specific, like two hundred and fifty-six or one thousand and twenty-four, look for the doubling underneath it. It is almost always there.

Which brings us to the most famous group of bits in the world, the byte. A byte is a group of 8 bits, always eight, no exceptions. It is the standard bundle, the way a dozen is a standard bundle of twelve eggs. When people talk about the size of a file or the memory of a phone, they count in bytes and in bundles of bytes, and we will meet those bigger bundles in lesson three. For now, the byte itself. Eight bits, each one zero or one. How many different values can a byte hold? Double two, eight times. Two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four, one hundred and twenty-eight, two hundred and fifty-six. A byte holds 256 different values, the numbers from zero up to 255. That number, two hundred and fifty-six, is going to follow us through this entire course. You will meet it in letters, in colours, in sound. When you see it, you will know what it means. Eight switches. Two hundred and fifty-six combinations.

So a computer counts, and it counts in binary, and it stores its counts in bytes. But counting alone does not give you a photograph or a letter to your sister. Numbers by themselves are just numbers. Here is the turn in the road, and it is the most important idea in this lesson, so I will say it slowly. The trick is representation. Representation means using numbers to stand for other things, by an agreed code. A code, in this sense, is simply an agreement. We agree that a certain number means a certain letter, and then whenever the machine stores that number, we read it as that letter. The number does not look like the letter. It does not need to. The agreement does all the work.

Let me work the set problem for this class in full, right now, the way I promised I would, because this problem looks small and it opens like a trapdoor. The problem is this. A computer is just counting with electricity, so what has to be added to counting before you get a word processor? Keep every claim checkable. Here is the worked answer, in four parts. Counting gives you numbers. You must add representation, numbers standing for letters, colours, and sounds by agreed codes. You must add stored instructions, the program kept as data the machine can fetch, and we will spend all of lesson four on that. You must add conditional branching, which means do this if that, the machine choosing its next step based on what it finds. And you must add input and output, a way for the world to reach the counting and for the counting to reach the world, a keyboard and a screen. A word processor is those four things, wearing a friendly face. Counting, plus representation, plus stored instructions, plus branching, plus input and output. That is the shape of every program you will ever use, and today we are mastering the first two parts of it, counting and representation.

So let us see representation at work with letters, because letters are where a word processor begins. There is an old and famous agreed code for letters, and its name is ASCII. You say it like askee. In ASCII, every letter and every common symbol is given a number, and the machine stores the number and trusts the agreement. In that code, the capital letter A is the number 65. The capital letter B is the number 66. The capital letter C is the number 67. The small letter a is the number 97. A space, the empty gap between words, is the number 32. A full stop is the number 46. So when you type the word CAB into your phone, the phone does not store anything that looks like letters. It stores three numbers, sixty-seven, sixty-five, and sixty-six, one byte each, and the screen draws the letters back for you because the screen is following the same agreement. Your whole message, every word of it, is a row of numbers under the surface. The letters are a kindness the machine does for your eyes.

And each of those numbers is itself stored in binary, in a byte, as eight switches. The letter A is sixty-five, and sixty-five in binary is 01000001. Read it with your method. The places are one hundred and twenty-eight, sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, eight, four, two, and one. The only ones in that row sit over sixty-four and over one, and sixty-four plus one is sixty-five. So the letter A, at the very bottom, is one byte where the sixty-four switch and the one switch are on and every other switch is off. When you press the A key on your phone, that is what you are really doing. You are setting eight switches in a pattern that the whole world of computing has agreed to read as A. I find that beautiful, and I am not embarrassed to say so. The grandest library ever built will rest on rows of switches just like that one.

Letters are only the beginning of representation. Colours work the same way, and once you see it, you will never look at a photograph on your phone the same way again. A photograph on a screen is made of tiny dots, and each dot is called a pixel, which is just a short way of saying picture element. The colour of each pixel is stored as three numbers, one for how much red is in it, one for how much green, and one for how much blue. Each of those three numbers is stored in one byte, so each one runs from zero up to two hundred and fifty-five. Zero red, zero green, and zero blue gives you black. Two hundred and fifty-five of all three gives you white. Two hundred and fifty-five red, zero green, and zero blue gives you a pure, strong red. Mix them in between and you can make any colour your eye can name. How many colours in total? Two hundred and fifty-six choices for red, times two hundred and fifty-six for green, times two hundred and fifty-six for blue, and the total is 16777216 different colours, more than sixteen million, from three bytes per dot. Three bytes. Twenty-four switches. Sixteen million colours. That is representation doing heavy lifting, and it is the same trick as the letters, numbers standing for something else by agreement.

Sound is representation too. A sound is a wave, a wiggle in the air, and a computer stores music by measuring that wiggle thousands of times every second and writing down each measurement as a number. Play the numbers back in order, at the same speed, and the wiggle is rebuilt and your ear hears the song. The voice you are listening to right now reached you exactly that way, as numbers, measured and rebuilt. Photographs, songs, letters, videos. Different agreements, same foundation. Numbers all the way down to the switches, and switches all the way up to the things you love.

Let me bring this home to your own life, because an idea you cannot use is an idea you do not yet own. Your phone, the one in your pocket, is a counting machine that never stops. When its screen says a photograph takes up three megabytes, it is telling you that the agreements for that picture, its pixels and colours, took about three million bytes to write down. When a message from your business arrives, it arrives as bytes, numbers for letters, flying as electricity and light. When your phone feels slow and someone tells you it needs more memory, they are talking about how many bytes it can keep close at hand, and that is lesson three, so hold the thought. For today, just notice this. Nothing in that phone is stored as the thing itself. There are no tiny letters hiding inside it and no tiny photographs. There are only numbers, stored as patterns of high and low electricity, waiting to be read back through the right agreement. If you understand that sentence, you understand the ground floor of computing, and most people who use computers every day of their lives have never once been told it.

One more small thing before we recap, because it will save you confusion later. People who work with computers often talk about bigger bundles of bytes, and the names sound alike. A kilobyte is a bundle of bytes, roughly one thousand of them, and in the strict counting we will use in this course it is 1024 bytes, which is two doubled ten times. A megabyte is roughly a million bytes. A gigabyte is roughly a billion bytes. Your phone probably holds one hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes or more, which is more than a hundred billion bytes, each one eight switches. The exact bundles get their own careful treatment in lesson three. For now, hear the rhythm of it. Byte, then thousands of bytes, then millions, then billions, and at every level it is still the same humble bit underneath, the single choice between zero and one.

Let us recap, in order, the way we built it. First, a bit is one single choice between two values, zero and one, and inside the machine that choice is carried by electricity, high for one and low for zero, because two far-apart states are almost impossible to misread. Second, binary is counting based on two, and its places are worth one, two, four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two, each double the last, and you read a binary number by multiplying each digit by its place and adding. Third, every extra bit doubles the number of values, so 5 bits give you 32 values and 10 bits give you 1024 values, and your own two hands proved it. Fourth, a byte is 8 bits and holds 256 values, from zero to 255. Fifth, representation is the great trick, numbers standing for letters, colours, and sounds by agreed codes, so the letter A is the number 65 and a pixel is three numbers that agree to be a colour. And sixth, counting alone is not a computer program. Add representation, stored instructions, conditional branching, and input and output, and counting becomes a word processor. Six points. If those six are clear in your mind, this lesson has done its work.

Next, in lesson two, we meet the worker who does all of this counting, the processor, a very fast and very literal clerk who follows instructions billions of times a second and never once uses his own judgment. He is a wonderful character and a cautionary tale, and you will like him.

But first, your questions on this lesson. They are waiting for you now, ten or so of them, about what I actually taught you here and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and I mean this exactly as I say it. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. If a question asks you about the value of a byte or the meaning of a bit, scroll back, find the line, and take the answer from the lesson itself. That is what the text is for. Work through them slowly, in order, easy ones first. You counted to thirty-one on one hand today. The questions will feel well within your reach. I will see you in lesson two.

lessons.title: The processor: a very fast, very literal clerk
paragraphs: Welcome back. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations. This is lesson two, and its title is The processor: a very fast, very literal clerk. In lesson one, you learned what the computer stores. Bits, bytes, numbers standing for letters and colours by agreed codes. Today you meet the worker who does something with all those stored numbers. Every computer has one, your phone has one, and by the end of this lesson you will know exactly what he does, how fast he does it, and why you must never, ever blame him for faithfully following a foolish instruction. He has no judgment. That is not an insult. It is his job description, and understanding it will save you from a hundred confusions later.

Let me unpack the title first, the way I like to do, piece by piece. Very. Fast. Literal. Clerk. Four words, and each one earns its place. A clerk is a person who works through paperwork, step by step, following written instructions, fetching what is needed, doing what the paper says, and filing the result. That is the processor. The word processor itself, in this lesson, does not mean the writing program from lesson one. Here, the processor is a piece of hardware, a chip, the working part of the machine. Its full name is the central processing unit, and people shorten that to CPU. Central, because everything passes through it. Processing, because it works on what passes through. Unit, because it is one part among several in the whole machine. When you hear CPU from today onward, picture the clerk at his desk, and you will not go far wrong.

Here is the definition I want you to keep, word for word if you can. The processor is the part of the computer that follows instructions, one after another, exactly as they are written. Follows instructions. One after another. Exactly as written. There is no fourth idea hiding in that sentence, and the third idea, exactly as written, is the one that runs the world. We will spend a good part of this lesson on what exactly as written really means, because it explains both the power of computers and most of their famous failures.

First, what does the clerk actually do all day? His whole working life is one small cycle of 3 steps, repeated without pause. The steps have names, and the names are plain. Fetch. Decode. Execute. Say them with me. Fetch, decode, execute. Fetch, decode, execute. That loop is the heartbeat of every computer ever built, and we are going to take each step slowly.

Fetch means the clerk gets the next instruction. The instructions live in the computer's memory, which is lesson three's territory, so for today just picture a long numbered row of pigeonholes, each one holding either a number or an instruction. The clerk keeps a note of where he is in that row. That note has a name, and the name is the program counter. The program counter is simply the clerk's note of which instruction comes next, the number of the pigeonhole he should visit. Fetch means he walks to that pigeonhole, takes out the instruction written there, and brings it back to his desk. Then, as a matter of routine, he updates his note to point at the next pigeonhole, so he is ready for the next fetch. Small step. Utterly reliable. Done billions of times without a sigh.

Decode means the clerk works out what the instruction is asking for. Remember from lesson one that everything inside the machine is numbers, and instructions are no exception. An instruction arrives at the desk as a number, a pattern of bits in a byte or a few bytes. Part of that pattern is a code number that names the job to be done, and the rest of the pattern names what to do the job on. Decode is the moment the clerk looks at the code number and says, in effect, ah, this is an adding instruction, and these are the two numbers it wants me to add. There is a fixed list of jobs the clerk knows how to do, and that list is called the instruction set. The instruction set is the complete list of jobs a processor can be told to do, and it is not long. Adding. Subtracting. Comparing two numbers to see which is bigger. Copying a number from one place to another. Jumping to a different instruction when a condition holds, which is the conditional branching you met in lesson one. A few dozen kinds of jobs, a few hundred at the most, and every program you have ever used, every game, every message, every photograph being shown, is built by stringing those few simple jobs together in enormous, careful crowds. Complexity in computing never comes from complicated steps. It comes from simple steps, numbered in the billions, arranged with great care.

Execute means the clerk does the job. If the instruction said add, he adds, using a part of the chip built for arithmetic, and he puts the answer in a small holding place on his own desk. Those holding places have a name too. They are called registers. A register is one of the processor's own tiny storage slots, the fastest storage in the whole machine, sitting right where the work happens. Think of the difference between the top of your desk and a warehouse across town. Registers are the top of the desk. Only a handful of numbers fit there, the ones being worked on right now, but the clerk can reach them instantly, because they are already in his hands. Execute, put the result in a register or send it back to memory, and then the cycle begins again. Fetch the next instruction. Decode it. Execute it. Fetch, decode, execute, for as long as the machine is switched on and there are instructions to follow.

Let me work a tiny example in full, because nobody should have to guess what this looks like when it runs. Picture a short program of 4 instructions, stored in memory, whose whole job is to add two numbers and keep the answer. The numbers we will add are seven and five, and you already know the answer is twelve, which is exactly why I chose them. A worked example should use numbers you can check, so you can watch the clerk instead of worrying about the arithmetic.

Instruction one says, fetch the number seven from memory and put it in a register. The clerk fetches the instruction, decodes it, and executes it, and now his first register holds seven. Instruction two says, fetch the number five from memory and put it in a second register. Fetch, decode, execute. The second register holds five. Instruction three says, add the two registers together and put the answer in the first register. Fetch, decode, execute. The adding part of the chip takes seven and five and makes twelve, and the first register now holds twelve. Instruction four says, copy the number in the first register back into memory, so the answer is kept. Fetch, decode, execute. Twelve is stored. The program ends. Four instructions, twelve steps of the cycle, and the machine has done a sum.

Now, that might sound like a lot of ceremony for seven plus five, and at human speed it is. You did that sum in your head before I finished the sentence. But notice what the ceremony buys. The clerk never gets bored. He never misreads a seven as a one because his eyes are tired. He never decides the answer is probably twelve and writes it down without adding. He does the steps, all the steps, every time, in order, and he does them the same way the billionth time as the first time. Give him a program of four instructions and he is a toy. Give him a program of four billion instructions and he is your phone, drawing your photographs, checking your spelling, and guiding you down the highway, all of it fetch, decode, execute, all the way down. Same clerk. Same three steps. Just more of them, and faster than you can imagine. Which brings us to the word fast, and I do mean very fast.
How fast is the clerk? Let us build the answer honestly, in stages, because the final number is so large that it means nothing until you climb up to it.

A good human clerk, working carefully with paper, might complete one simple instruction every few seconds. Say one instruction in one second, to be generous, and to keep the arithmetic clean. One per second. Now, the processor in an ordinary modern phone or laptop completes billions of instructions in that same second. Not thousands. Not millions. Billions. To make that word into a number you can hold, the speed of a processor is measured by its clock. The clock is the heartbeat of the processor, a steady tick that keeps every step in time. Each tick of the clock is called a cycle, and in each cycle the clerk can complete a step of his work, sometimes a whole simple instruction, sometimes part of one. Clock speeds are measured in a unit called the hertz, which simply means times per second. One hertz is one tick per second. The processors in modern machines tick at around 3 gigahertz. Giga means billion, so 3 gigahertz means the clock ticks 3000000000 times every second. Three billion ticks. Every second. While you read this sentence aloud, the clerk in your phone has ticked more times than there are seconds in your whole life so far. I am not exaggerating for effect. That is the plain arithmetic of three billion ticks a second against the eighty or so years a long life contains.

Here is a comparison I use with every class, because it finally makes the speed felt. Imagine the clerk worked at human speed, one instruction per second, and we asked him to run a program of 3000000000 instructions, a program your phone handles in about a second. At one per second, that program would take 3000000000 seconds. There are about thirty million seconds in a year, so the human clerk would need roughly one hundred years to finish what your phone does while you blink. And the machine clerk does not need the hundred years, or the coffee, or the sleep. He needs the second. When people say computers are fast, this is the size of the word fast that they mean. The clerk is not cleverer than you. He is not clever at all. He is simply tireless at a speed that turns patience into power, because a simple job done three billion times a second stops being a simple job. It becomes a photograph appearing, a voice being recognised, a business being run.

Now the other word in the title, and in some ways the more important one. Literal. The clerk does exactly what the instruction says. Not what the instruction meant. Not what a sensible person would have understood. What it says. If the instruction contains a mistake, the clerk will carry out the mistake at full speed, three billion times a second, without pausing to wonder whether the result looks odd. He has no common sense, because common sense was never in his job description. His job description is fetch, decode, execute, and there is no fourth step called think about whether this is wise.

Let me give you the classic classroom example, and then it is your turn to try it, because this idea is learned by doing and not by watching. Suppose you ask a friend to make you a sandwich, and you give the instruction, put the peanut butter on the bread. Your friend, being a person, understands everything you did not say. Open the jar first. Use a knife. Spread it on one side. A reasonable amount. Now imagine giving that same instruction to our clerk, who understands nothing that is not written down. Put the peanut butter on the bread. He takes the sealed jar and sets it down on top of the loaf. Done. Instruction executed, exactly as written. You protest, and he is innocent, and he is right to be innocent, because the instruction was wrong, not the clerk. Every missing detail in an instruction is a place where the literal clerk will surprise you, and he will surprise you in the direction of the words you actually gave him.

This is your guided moment, so do it properly. Think of one small job from your own daily life, something you could explain to a person in one sentence. Making a cup of tea. Buttering toast. Locking up the house at night. Now rewrite that one sentence as instructions for the clerk, and keep asking yourself, at every single step, what have I assumed that I have not said? Where is the kettle in your instructions? Did you say to fill it? Did you say with water? Did you say to wait until it boils, and how would the clerk know it has boiled? Most people find, within five steps, that their simple job needs twenty instructions and still has gaps. That feeling, that slight dizziness at how much a person carries in their head without noticing, is the true beginning of understanding programs. Programs are what you get when someone does this work completely, closing every gap, for jobs thousands or millions of steps long. Lesson four is devoted to that, and you will be ready for it, because you will have felt in your own kitchen why it is hard.

There is a famous saying in computing that belongs here, and it is short enough to remember whole. Garbage in, garbage out. It means that if the instructions or the numbers given to the machine are wrong, the answers coming out will be wrong too, no matter how fast or expensive the machine is. The clerk does not launder bad work into good work. He amplifies whatever he is given, wisdom or folly, at three billion steps a second. When a computer produces a wrong bill, a wrong date, a wrong total for your business, the machine is almost never lying and almost never broken. Somewhere upstream, a human wrote an instruction that said the wrong thing, or fed it a wrong number, and the clerk, faithful as ever, executed it exactly. Blaming the clerk is like blaming a mirror for a stain on your shirt. The mirror's whole virtue is that it shows what is in front of it, and the clerk's whole virtue is the same.

Now, one more piece of the picture before we recap, because modern processors have a trick that the single-clerk picture does not show. One clerk, however fast, can only be in one place in the instruction row at a time. So modern chips put several clerks on the same desk. Each complete clerk inside a processor is called a core. A core is a full working processor inside the processor, able to fetch, decode, and execute its own stream of instructions. Many phones today have 8 cores. That means eight clerks, working side by side on different parts of the job at the same moment. One core draws your screen while another handles your music and a third watches for your messages arriving. When a machine is described as having more cores, it is not a faster clerk. It is more clerks. Speed of each worker and number of workers are two different kinds of power, and advertisements love to blur them. You will not blur them, because you have the picture. Ticks per second tell you how fast each clerk works. Cores tell you how many clerks there are.

And where do the instructions and numbers come from, at that speed? The clerk's desk, his registers, holds only a handful of numbers. Everything else, the programs and the data they work on, lives in memory and storage, the desk and the filing cabinet of lesson three. The clerk spends his life fetching from that memory, and how far away the memory sits is one of the great practical questions in all of computing. Hold that thought. It is literally the next lesson.

Let me also place the clerk honestly among his colleagues, because you will hear other chip names and I do not want them to blur together. The processor we have described, the general clerk, is good at following any instructions in order. There is a cousin chip that specialises in drawing pictures, doing the same small calculation on millions of pixels at once, and it matters greatly for games and for the AI work later in this path. Its name can wait. For today, the lesson is the clerk himself, the general worker, the one who runs the show, fetches every instruction, and answers for everything the machine does. In most machines, most of the time, if something happened, the clerk did it, following orders.

Before we recap, let me show you the clerk handling the one job that makes him more than a calculator, because it is the job lesson one's worked answer promised you. Conditional branching. Branching means the clerk does not always march to the very next instruction. Sometimes an instruction tells him, if a condition holds, jump ahead or jump back to a different part of the program. Picture the program counter again, the clerk's note of what comes next. A branch is an instruction that rewrites that note. Instead of moving to the next pigeonhole, the clerk crosses out his note and writes a new address, and his next fetch goes there instead.

Here is a small, complete example you can follow on your fingers. Suppose a program is counting down from three, the way a timer does. An instruction subtracts one from a number in a register. The next instruction says, if the register is not yet zero, jump back and subtract again. The next instruction after that says the counting is finished. Now run the clerk through it. The register starts at three. Subtract, and it holds two. Is it zero? No. Jump back. Subtract, and it holds one. Is it zero? No. Jump back. Subtract, and it holds zero. Is it zero? Yes. Do not jump. Move on to the finished instruction. That tiny loop, subtract and test and jump, is the seed of almost everything interesting a computer does. Searching a list is a loop. Drawing a photograph is loops inside loops, one for every row of pixels. Waiting for you to tap the screen is a loop that tests, and tests, and tests, until the test finally says yes. When the clerk jumps, he is not being clever. The instruction told him exactly when to jump and exactly where to land. But the effect of all that faithful jumping is a machine that can handle situations its programmer never counted by hand, because the counting, the testing, and the choosing were built into the instructions themselves.

Notice, too, what the branch is made of. The decision rests on a comparison, and a comparison is one of the clerk's ordinary jobs from his instruction set. Is this number bigger than that one? Are these two numbers equal? Is this register zero yet? The clerk answers with a simple result, in effect yes or no, one bit of truth, and the branch instruction spends that bit immediately. Lesson one's humble bit, the single choice between two values, turns out to steer the whole machine. Bits store the numbers. Bits store the instructions. And a single bit, freshly minted by a comparison, decides which road the program walks next. That is a satisfying piece of architecture, and it is worth pausing on, because nothing in this course is wasted. Everything you learn here returns later, wearing a bigger coat.

One honest warning grows straight out of the branch, and every programmer learns it the hard way. If the test in a loop can never come out the way the instruction expects, the clerk will loop forever. He will subtract, test, jump, subtract, test, jump, three billion times a second, patient as stone, waiting for a condition that the instructions themselves made impossible. The machine has not crashed in the sense of breaking. It is doing exactly what it was told, forever. When your phone freezes on one screen and will not answer, very often some clerk inside it is running a faithful, endless errand of exactly this kind. The cure people reach for, turning it off and on again, works because it wipes the clerk's note and makes him start from the very first instruction of a known program. Keep that in mind for your own machines. A frozen device is usually not a dead device. It is a literal clerk, trapped by literal instructions, waiting for someone to hand him a fresh start.

Two questions follow naturally, and a good student asks both, so let us take them before we close. The first is, if speed is so wonderful, why not simply make the clock tick faster and faster forever? Because the clerk works in the physical world, and the physical world charges for speed. Every tick moves electricity through tiny paths, and moving electricity makes heat. Tick twice as fast and you make roughly twice the heat in the same small space. A chip is smaller than your thumbnail, and at modern speeds it can produce more heat for its size than a stove element. That is why laptops have fans, why phones grow warm in your hand when they work hard, and why the clerk sometimes slows himself down on purpose when he gets hot, a behaviour called throttling. Your phone is not being lazy when it slows on a hot day. Its clerk is protecting himself from cooking. Speed in computing is always bought with heat and battery, and the art of the engineer is spending both wisely.

The second question is closer to your own work. If the clerk is this fast and this faithful, why do programs still feel slow, and why do computers still make mistakes with your business files and your messages? Because the clerk is rarely the slow part. He waits. He waits for memory to hand him the next instruction, waits for storage to deliver a photograph, waits for the network to bring a message from across the country. A clerk who can work in a billionth of a second, waiting on deliveries that take a thousand times longer, spends most of his life waiting, and lessons three and five are about those two waits. And the mistakes, as the sandwich taught us, are almost never his. They live in the instructions, written by people, in a hurry, with assumptions they never noticed they were making. Understanding the clerk teaches you where to look when a machine misbehaves. Not at the faithful worker. At the orders he was handed, and at the numbers he was fed. That habit of mind, looking upstream for the real cause, is worth more than any single fact in this lesson, and it will serve you in every lesson that follows and in a good deal of life outside this classroom as well.

Let us recap, in order. First, the processor, or CPU, is the part of the computer that follows instructions, one after another, exactly as they are written. Second, his whole life is a cycle of 3 steps, fetch, decode, and execute, repeated without pause. Third, fetch uses the program counter, the clerk's note of which instruction comes next. Fourth, decode reads the instruction as a number and matches its code against the instruction set, the fixed list of jobs he knows. Fifth, execute does the job, and the numbers being worked on sit in registers, the tiny, fastest storage on the clerk's own desk. Sixth, he is very fast. His clock ticks about 3000000000 times a second, at around 3 gigahertz, and that speed turns simple steps into enormous power. Seventh, he is very literal. He does what the instruction says, never what it meant, which is why garbage in means garbage out. And eighth, modern processors hold several clerks at once, each one called a core, and many phones have 8 cores working side by side.

Next lesson, lesson three, we walk out of the clerk's office and look at where everything is kept. Memory and storage, the desk and the filing cabinet, why your phone can forget an app in a blink but keeps your photographs for years, and why the difference matters every day.

First, your questions on this lesson. They cover what I taught here, the cycle, the speed, the literal clerk, and nothing I did not teach. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. Find the line, take the answer from the lesson, and move on with confidence. If the sandwich example comes back to you while you answer, smile. It means the lesson is working. I will see you in lesson three.

lessons.title: Memory and storage: the desk and the filing cabinet
paragraphs: Welcome back. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations. This is lesson three, and its title is Memory and storage: the desk and the filing cabinet. In lesson one you learned what the computer stores, numbers in bits and bytes, standing for letters and colours and sounds. In lesson two you met the clerk, the processor, who follows instructions at three billion ticks a second. Today we answer the question the clerk himself kept asking. Where does he fetch all those instructions and numbers from? Where is everything kept? The answer comes in two parts, and the difference between the two parts explains some of the most familiar mysteries of daily life with machines. Why does your phone remember your photographs for years but forget an unsaved note in a blink? Why can it hold thousands of pictures but only a handful of open apps? Why does a bigger number on the box sometimes matter and sometimes not? By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain all three, in plain language, to anyone who asks.

Here is the picture, and it is the picture in the title. Think of the processor as the clerk from lesson two, sitting at work. Every worker needs two kinds of space. He needs a desk, right in front of him, where the papers he is working on right now are spread out where his hands can reach them. And he needs a filing cabinet, across the room, where the records he is not using today are kept safe, in far greater quantity than any desk could hold. A computer has exactly the same two kinds of space, and confusing them is the single most common confusion in all of computing. Today we separate them forever.

The desk is called memory. When people who work with computers say memory, they almost always mean one specific thing, and its short name is RAM. RAM stands for random access memory, and I will unpack that name in a moment, because it is less frightening than it sounds. For now, hold the picture. Memory is the computer's desk, fast and close, where the work in progress sits, and everything on it vanishes when the power goes. Read that sentence again, slowly, because it carries the whole lesson. Fast and close. Work in progress. Vanishes when the power goes. Three claims, and we will take them one at a time.

Fast and close first. The clerk works at billions of ticks a second, and he cannot spend those ticks walking across town. The desk is built right around him, wired tightly to him, so that when he reaches for an instruction or a number, it is in his hands almost immediately. Almost immediately, at computer scale, means a few billionths of a second. That speed is not a luxury. It is a necessity. A clerk who ticks three billion times a second, fed by a slow desk, would spend nearly all of his life sitting idle with his hands folded, waiting for the next paper to arrive. Lesson two warned you that the clerk spends much of his life waiting. The desk exists to make the most common waits as short as physics allows.

Work in progress second. What actually sits on the desk at any moment? Exactly what is being worked on, and nothing else. The program that is running right now, with its instructions laid out in order so the clerk can fetch them one by one. The numbers that program is using. The photograph you have open, decoded from its stored numbers into pixels ready to draw. The message you are halfway through typing. The song that is playing this second. If a thing is in use, it is on the desk. If it is not in use, it is not on the desk, because the desk is not big enough for everything, and it was never meant to be. That is not a flaw in the design. That is the design. A desk is for today's work.

Vanishes when the power goes, third, and this is the claim people find hardest to believe, so let me be very plain. The desk forgets. Memory holds its bits as tiny electrical charges and patterns that must be kept alive by power. The moment the power stops, the charges drain away, and every bit on the desk falls back to nothing. The technical word for this behaviour is volatile. A thing is volatile if it disappears when the power goes. Memory is volatile. That is why, when your phone battery dies in the middle of an unsaved note, the note is gone. It was never anywhere but the desk, and the desk went dark. That is why a laptop that loses power can lose the last paragraph you typed but never loses the document you saved an hour ago. The saved document was in the cabinet. The paragraph was only on the desk. Same machine, two kinds of space, two different fates, and now you know which is which.

Now the name, quickly, because I promised. Random access memory. Access means reaching something. Random, in this one technical sense, does not mean haphazard or by chance. It means the clerk can reach any spot on the desk directly, in any order, just as fast as any other spot. He does not have to start at one end and walk. Every pigeonhole on the desk is the same short reach away. That is what random access means, and it is a large part of why the desk is fast. Compare a roll of tape, where reaching the middle means winding through everything before it. The desk is not a tape. The desk is a desk. Any paper, any moment, same reach.

How big is the desk? Desks in modern machines are measured in gigabytes, and you met the gigabyte in lesson one as roughly a billion bytes. A typical modern phone has 8 gigabytes of memory. Eight billion bytes, give or take, spread out on the desk. A decent laptop might have 16 gigabytes, and a heavy working machine 32 gigabytes or more. Hold those numbers loosely for now. What matters is the comparison that is coming, because the filing cabinet is measured in the same units, and it dwarfs the desk every single time.

Now walk across the room with me to the filing cabinet. The cabinet is called storage. Storage is the filing cabinet, slower and far bigger, where things are kept when nobody is working on them, and it keeps them through the dark. Again, three claims in one sentence, and again we take them in order. Slower. Far bigger. Keeps them through the dark.

Slower first, and slower needs honest handling, because storage is not slow the way a person is slow. Reaching into storage takes the clerk perhaps a hundred times longer than reaching the desk, sometimes more. At human scale both feel instant. At the clerk's scale, where a billionth of a second is a working lifetime, a hundredfold wait is an age. That is the whole reason the desk exists. If storage were as fast as memory, we would build the whole machine out of it and this lesson would be one paragraph long. It is not, so we do not, and the two-tier system, small fast desk and huge slower cabinet, is the compromise every computer on Earth has settled on.

Far bigger second. Where the phone's desk is 8 gigabytes, the same phone's cabinet is commonly 128 gigabytes, or 256 gigabytes, sixteen or thirty-two times the size of the desk. Laptops carry storage of 512 gigabytes or a full terabyte, and a terabyte is roughly a trillion bytes, a thousand gigabytes. Your business files, your photographs, your music, your apps themselves when they are not running, all of it lives in the cabinet, and the cabinet has room for a life's worth of it. When an advertisement shouts a big number of gigabytes at you, it is almost always shouting about the cabinet, because the cabinet's number is the big one. Now you will know to ask the second question. How big is the desk? That number decides how much work the machine can hold open at once, and it is printed much smaller, when it is printed at all.

Keeps them through the dark, third, and this is storage's great virtue. Storage holds its bits in a way that does not need power to survive. In a phone and in most modern laptops, storage is a kind of chip called flash memory, which traps tiny charges in a way that stays put for years without power. In older and larger machines, storage is a spinning disc with a magnetic surface, called a hard drive, where the bits are written as magnetic patterns that likewise stay where they were put. Either way, the principle is the same, and the technical word for it is non-volatile. Non-volatile means it does not disappear when the power goes. Turn the phone off. Leave it in a drawer for a year. Turn it on, and your photographs are still there, because they were in the cabinet, and the cabinet keeps its records through the dark. That is the promise that makes storage storage.

Now let me put the two together in one ordinary moment from your own life, worked in full, because this is the kind of thing I want you to be able to trace without me. You tap the icon of your photo app. What happens, step by step? The app itself, as a program, lives in the cabinet, in storage, where it has been sitting since you installed it. Tapping the icon is an instruction to bring that program to the desk. The machine copies the program from storage into memory, onto the desk, and only then can the clerk start fetching its instructions, because the clerk fetches from the desk. That small delay while the app opens, the pause you feel, is largely the sound of papers being carried across the room. Then you tap one photograph. That photograph's numbers also live in the cabinet. They are copied to the desk, decoded there into millions of coloured pixels, and the clerk and his colleagues draw them on the screen. You edit the photograph, cropping it, brightening it. Your edits happen on the desk, in memory, at full clerk speed. And then, the moment that matters most. You press save. Save means, carry this finished work from the desk back to the cabinet and write it there. Until you press save, your edits exist only on the volatile desk. After save, they are in the non-volatile cabinet, and they will survive the battery dying, the phone falling, the year in the drawer. Save is not a courtesy button. Save is the walk across the room, and now you know exactly what it does and why it matters.

This also explains the mystery of the vanishing app. You open six apps on your phone, one after another, and when you return to the first one, it starts over from the beginning, as if you had never been there. Nothing is broken. The desk filled up. Six apps, each with its work spread out, is more paper than the desk can hold, so the machine quietly cleared the oldest app's papers back off the desk to make room. The app itself is safe in the cabinet. Its work in progress, the half-typed message, the paused place in the article, was on the desk, and the desk was needed for something else. A bigger desk, more memory, means more apps can keep their work spread out at once. That, and nothing else, is what the memory number on the box is really promising you.

Now the bundles, carefully, because you will meet these numbers on every box and every bill for the rest of your life, and I want them demystified. Bytes come in bundles, and in this course we count the bundles the strict way, the way the machine counts. 1 kilobyte is 1024 bytes. 1 megabyte is 1024 kilobytes, which is 1048576 bytes. 1 gigabyte is 1024 megabytes. 1 terabyte is 1024 gigabytes. You will notice the number 1024 everywhere, and by now you can guess why. It is two doubled ten times, the closest power of two to a thousand, and lesson one's doubling pattern is still running the show. When a person says a file is about a megabyte, they mean about a million bytes, and for everyday talk that rounding is fine. But when you are counting what fits where, the strict numbers are the ones that add up.

Here is your guided moment, a piece of arithmetic from real life, and I want you to actually do it, out loud if you can. Suppose your phone tells you it has 8 gigabytes of free storage, and suppose each photograph you take takes up about 4 megabytes. How many more photographs can the phone hold? Work it the way we worked the binary numbers, in steps. Step one, turn the gigabytes into megabytes. One gigabyte is 1024 megabytes, so 8 gigabytes is 8 times 1024, which is 8192 megabytes. Step two, divide by the size of one photograph. 8192 divided by 4 is 2048. Your phone can hold about 2048 more photographs. Two thousand and forty-eight photographs, in the space a quick glance calls eight gigabytes. That is what the cabinet's numbers mean when you unfold them, and you unfolded them yourself, with nothing but the bundles and one division. Keep the method. Free space, turned into the same units as the thing you want to store, divided by the size of the thing. It works for photographs, for songs, for business files, for anything made of bytes, which after lesson one you know means everything.

Now I can show you something beautiful, because you have all the pieces. The desk and the cabinet are not the whole story. They are the middle of a ladder, and the ladder is one of the great organising ideas of computing. You already know the top rung. In lesson two, the clerk's own registers, the tiny slots in his hands, holding the few numbers being worked on at this exact tick. Below the registers sits a small, extremely fast store built into the processor itself, called the cache. The cache is the processor's private shelf, a small fast store that keeps copies of the instructions and numbers the clerk is most likely to need next, so he does not have to reach even as far as the desk. Below the cache, the desk itself, memory, gigabytes of it, a few billionths of a second away. And below the desk, across the room, the cabinet, storage, hundreds of gigabytes, a hundred times slower to reach, keeping everything through the dark.

Small and fast at the top. Huge and slow at the bottom. Every rung bigger and slower than the rung above it. That shape is not an accident and it is not a fashion. It is forced on us by physics and by price. The fastest kinds of storage are the most expensive per byte and the hardest to build in bulk, so we build a little of them. The slowest kinds are cheap per byte, so we build mountains of them. The ladder is how a machine pretends, convincingly, to be both enormous and instant. The clerk works at the top. The copies flow up and down the ladder as needed. When the system works well, the thing the clerk wants next is almost always already on the shelf or the desk, and the long walk to the cabinet is rare. When it works badly, when the desk is too small for the job, the clerk spends his billions of ticks waiting on the stairs, and the whole machine feels slow even though its clerk is a marvel. If you remember one sentence from this lesson when you are buying a machine or judging one, make it this one. A computer feels fast when the work fits the desk, and slow when it does not.

There is one more trick the machine uses when the desk overflows, and you should know it because it explains a particular kind of slowness you have certainly felt. When memory fills completely, the machine begins using a corner of the cabinet as if it were extra desk space, carrying papers back and forth between the real desk and the cabinet as the clerk needs them. This overflow arrangement is called swap, because the machine is forever swapping papers in and out. It works, in the sense that the job gets done and nothing is lost. But remember the price of the walk. The cabinet is a hundred times slower to reach, so a machine living in swap is a clerk spending his day on the stairs, and everything about it feels like wading. When an old computer grinds and stutters while doing several things at once, this is very often the honest explanation. Not a broken clerk. A full desk, and a long walk, repeated a million times. The cure is a bigger desk or less work spread out at once, and now you can say why, in plain words, instead of just feeling that the machine is tired.

Let me bring the whole lesson home to your own machines and your own files, because this is a class about your life as much as about chips. Your business records, your customer lists, your photographs of finished work, the documents you cannot afford to lose. Ask of each one, where does it live? If the only copy is on the desk, in an open app, unsaved, it lives one power cut away from gone. If it is saved, it is in the cabinet of one machine, which is good, and the cabinet can still break, or the phone can still be lost, which is why lesson six will talk about copies in more than one place. For today, the habit to build is simpler. Save early, save often, and know what the button is doing when you press it. It is carrying your work across the room, from the fast forgetful desk to the slow faithful cabinet, and that walk is the difference between work that survives the night and work that does not.

One more distinction, drawn cleanly, because salespeople blur it and I will not have you blurred. Memory and storage are not two sizes of the same thing, and you cannot trade one for the other. A phone with a huge cabinet and a small desk will hold every photograph you ever take and still lose your place in every app. A machine with a huge desk and a small cabinet will juggle work beautifully and then run out of room to keep anything. When you choose a machine, you are choosing both numbers, for two different jobs. The desk for the work. The cabinet for the keeping. Say it that way to any salesperson and watch the conversation improve.

There is one everyday ceremony that shows the whole system at once, and you perform it without thinking. Turning the machine on. At the moment you press the button, the desk is empty, wiped clean by the time without power, because the desk is volatile. The clerk wakes to a bare desk and cannot begin, because he fetches his instructions from the desk and there is nothing on it. So the machine's first job, built into its deepest wiring, is to go to the cabinet and fetch the one program that starts all the others, the operating system, the program that runs the machine itself. You will meet the operating system properly in lesson four. For now, watch the walk. Cabinet to desk, program by program, the desk fills, the clerk begins fetching in earnest, and the screen comes alive. That pause while a machine starts, the logo, the spinning wheel, is the sound of a very large set of papers being carried across a room and laid out in order. And when you turn the machine off properly, the reverse courtesy happens. Programs are asked to save their work to the cabinet, desks are cleared in an orderly way, and only then does the power go. Pulling the plug skips the courtesy, which is why machines scold you about it, gently, the next time they wake.

The same ceremony explains the fullest cabinet mystery of all. When your phone warns you that storage is almost full, it is not being fussy. A cabinet with no free drawers cannot accept the walk. New photographs have nowhere to be filed, updated apps have nowhere to put their new selves, and the overflow space the machine uses for swap disappears as well. The phone slows, refuses, and complains, all from one cause. No room in the cabinet. The fix follows from the picture, as every fix in this class should. Delete what you no longer keep, or move the keeping to a bigger cabinet, which is part of what lesson six will mean by your data living in more than one place. A warning you understand is a warning you can act on, and you now understand this one all the way down to the bits.

One last worked trace, small and complete, because I want the two spaces working together in your mind before the questions. Imagine you are writing a message to a customer, a long one, with prices in it. You open the messaging app. The app travels from cabinet to desk and starts running. You type. Every letter you type is a number from lesson one, held for the moment in memory, on the desk, because the message is work in progress. The app, being well made, quietly saves a draft to the cabinet every so often, and that quiet saving is the walk happening without your asking. Your battery dies at the worst moment. The desk goes dark, and everything since the last quiet save is gone, but the draft in the cabinet survives, and when the phone wakes, the app walks it back to the desk and offers it to you. Nothing about that rescue is magic, and nothing about the loss is a betrayal. Two kinds of space did exactly what this lesson said they do. The desk held the work. The cabinet kept what was carried to it. If you can tell that story back to yourself without my voice, you own this lesson, and you are ready to be tested on it.

Let us recap, in order. First, memory is the computer's desk, fast and close, where the work in progress sits, and everything on it vanishes when the power goes. Second, that vanishing has a name, volatile, and it is why unsaved work dies with the battery. Third, RAM, random access memory, is the desk's proper name, and random access means any spot can be reached directly, just as fast as any other. Fourth, storage is the filing cabinet, slower and far bigger, where things are kept when nobody is working on them, and it keeps them through the dark. Fifth, storage is non-volatile, holding its bits through years without power, in flash chips or on magnetic discs. Sixth, save is the walk across the room, copying finished work from the desk to the cabinet. Seventh, the bundles run 1024 at a time. 1 kilobyte is 1024 bytes, 1 megabyte is 1024 kilobytes, 1 gigabyte is 1024 megabytes. And eighth, registers, cache, memory, and storage form a ladder, small and fast at the top, huge and slow at the bottom, and a machine feels fast when the work fits the desk.

Next lesson, lesson four, we finally open the question this whole course has been circling. Where do the instructions themselves come from? Programs, instructions all the way down, how the clerk's orders get written, stored, and turned into the apps you use. It is the heart of the course, and you are ready for it.

First, your questions on this lesson. They ask about the desk and the cabinet, the bundles, and the fate of unsaved work, and nothing I did not teach. Take them slowly. Several of them are the small arithmetic you practised with the photographs, and if the numbers blur, go back to the worked example and walk the steps again in the same order. That is not a weakness in your learning. That is the learning, happening the way it always happens in this room, by doing the thing again with your own hands until your hands know it. The full text stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. Find the line, take the answer from the lesson itself, and notice how much of your daily life with machines this one lesson has already explained. I will see you in lesson four.
