lessons.title: Programs: instructions all the way down
paragraphs: Welcome back. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations. This is lesson four, and its title is Programs: instructions all the way down. We have spent three lessons building the machine. Lesson one gave it numbers, bits and bytes standing for everything by agreed codes. Lesson two gave it a worker, the processor, the very fast and very literal clerk. Lesson three gave it places to keep things, the desk of memory and the filing cabinet of storage. Today we ask the question the whole course has been circling. Who writes the clerk's orders? Where do the instructions come from, and how does a machine that only understands numbers come to run something as human as a messaging app or a photo album? The answer is the program, and by the end of this lesson you will know what a program is, what an algorithm is, how human writing becomes machine numbers, and why the phrase instructions all the way down is not a joke but a precise description of reality.

Start with the definition, and keep it, because everything today hangs on it. A program is a set of instructions stored in memory, written in advance, that the processor fetches and follows one by one. Unpack it with me, the way we unpack things in this room. A set of instructions. Not a wish, not a goal, not a general direction. Instructions, each one small enough for the clerk's fixed list of jobs. Stored in memory. The instructions sit on the desk, in the same memory that holds the numbers, in the same form as the numbers, as patterns of bits. Written in advance. Someone, or something, wrote them before the clerk ever ran, and the clerk's job is not to invent them but to follow them. Fetches and follows one by one. Fetch, decode, execute, the cycle from lesson two, running on a list someone prepared.

That middle idea, stored in memory, deserves a pause, because it is one of the great inventions of the modern world and it hides in plain sight. The instructions are data. The program is kept in the same pigeonholes, in the same bytes, as the numbers it works on. The clerk fetches a byte and, depending on where he is in his work, that byte might be a number to add, a letter to display, or an instruction to obey. This is called the stored program idea, and it is what separates a computer from a calculator. A calculator's instructions are built into its wiring. It can only ever do the jobs it was born doing. A computer's instructions arrive as data, which means you can change what the machine is, entirely, by changing what is stored in its memory. Load one program and the phone is a camera. Load another and the same phone, the same clerk, the same desk, is a map, a bank, a piano, a business office. The hardware does not change at all. The instructions change, and the machine becomes a different machine. Every app you have ever installed was exactly that. New instructions, carried to the cabinet, loaded onto the desk, and the faithful clerk became something new without a single wire moving.

Now, where do the instructions come from? They are written by people, and the writing of them has a name you already know from ordinary speech. Programming. But before a program can be written, something more basic has to exist, and it has a name of its own. An algorithm is a method for solving a problem, written as a clear sequence of steps that always finishes and always gives the answer. Hold that definition next to the clerk and you will see they were made for each other. The clerk needs steps. The algorithm is steps. The clerk needs the steps to be unambiguous, because he is literal. The algorithm demands clarity for the same reason. And the algorithm must finish. A method that might wander forever is not an algorithm, it is a hope.

You already own algorithms, because a recipe is one. A recipe for bread is a sequence of steps, in order, with amounts, with tests along the way. Is the dough risen? Not yet, wait longer, test again. That test is a branch, the same branch the clerk makes. A recipe assumes a cook with judgment, who knows what knead means and what golden looks like. An algorithm for a computer assumes the clerk, who knows nothing that is not written down, so every recipe word must be replaced by exact operations from his little list. Add. Compare. Copy. Jump if. That translation, from human method to clerk-proof steps, is the daily work of the programmer, and it is harder and more interesting than it sounds, as the sandwich in lesson two already taught you.

Let me work a complete example in full, the way I promised this class would always work, so you can see an algorithm become a program and a program become a result. The problem is small and real. A customer has bought three things, and we want the total. The prices, in dollars, are 4, 9, and 2. You know the total is fifteen, and that is why I chose these numbers. Watch the method, not the arithmetic.

Here is the algorithm, in plain words first. Keep a running total, starting at zero. Take each price in turn. Add it to the total. When there are no prices left, the total is the answer. That is the whole method, and notice it would work for three prices or three thousand, unchanged. That is the mark of a real algorithm. It does not care how big the list is.

Now the program, written as instructions the clerk could follow. Instruction one. Put the number zero in a named place called total. Instruction two. Put the number zero in a named place called position, meaning which price we are looking at. Instruction three. If position has reached the end of the list, jump to the final instruction. Instruction four. Take the price at the current position and add it to total. Instruction five. Add one to position. Instruction six. Jump back to instruction three. And the final instruction. The number in total is the answer. Show it.

Those named places deserve their own sentence, because you will meet them in every program ever written. A variable is a named place in memory that holds a value, and the value can change as the program runs. Total is a variable. Position is a variable. The name stays the same, the number inside changes, and the program refers to the place by its name instead of by its address in the pigeonholes. A variable is a labelled box, and programming is, in large part, deciding what boxes you need and what goes in them.

Now run the clerk through the program, step by step, and watch the loop do its work. Total starts at zero, position at zero. Instruction three asks, is position at the end? The list has 3 prices, positions zero, one, and two, so no. Instruction four adds the price at position zero, which is 4. Total is now 4. Instruction five makes position one. Jump back. Is position at the end? No. Add the price at position one, which is 9. Total is now 13. Position becomes two. Jump back. At the end? No. Add the price at position two, which is 2. Total is now 15. Position becomes three. Jump back. Is position at the end now? Yes, three is past the last price. Jump to the final instruction. The answer is 15. The program stops, having added a list of prices, and it would stop with the right answer for any list you handed it. That little machine of seven instructions contains almost everything. Variables, a loop, a test, a branch, an answer. Scale it up, add pictures and buttons and sounds, and you have the apps on your phone. I do not say that loosely. I say it as a plain fact about how those apps are built.

But wait. There is a gap in that story, and a good student spots it. I wrote the program just now in plain English sentences. The clerk cannot read English. The clerk reads numbers, instruction codes from his instruction set, patterns of bits. So how does a program written by a person become the numbers the clerk obeys? This is the translation problem, and solving it is what made programming a craft that more than a handful of people could practise.

The first programmers had no choice but to write the numbers themselves. They wrote machine code, which is the program in its raw form, the actual instruction codes and addresses, number by number. It can be done. The first generation did it, heroically, and it was slow, and it was brutally easy to get wrong, because one wrong digit in a thousand numbers is invisible until the machine does something strange three billion steps later. Human beings are not built to write thousands of bare numbers without error. So we did what human beings always do. We built a tool to do the translating.

The tool rests on a simple, generous idea. Let people write programs in a language closer to human thinking, with words and names and tidy structures, and let a program do the work of turning that writing into machine code. A language of that kind is called a programming language. There are hundreds of them, with names like Python and JavaScript and C, and they differ the way human languages differ, in flavour and in what they are best at, but they share the essential bargain. The person writes in words a person can read and check. The machine receives numbers the clerk can execute. And between the two stands a translator, which is itself a program.

The translator comes in two main kinds, and the difference is worth knowing plainly. A compiler is a program that translates the whole of a human-written program into machine code before any of it runs. The whole book, translated cover to cover, and then the translation is what runs, as many times as you like, at full clerk speed. An interpreter is a program that translates the human-written program as it runs, piece by piece, fetching a line of the human writing, turning it into machine steps, doing them, and moving to the next line. The book is read aloud by a translator standing at your shoulder. Compiled programs generally run faster, because the translating is finished before the running starts. Interpreted programs are generally easier to change and test, because you can adjust the writing and run it again at once. Both are honest tools. Both end at the same place. Numbers, in memory, fetched by the clerk. Instructions all the way down is not a slogan. At the bottom of every layer of convenience, there is the clerk, and his numbers, and nothing else.

Notice what just happened, because it is the deepest pattern in this course. The translator is a program. The program that checks your spelling is a program. And underneath all of them sits one program with a special job, which you glimpsed in lesson three when the machine woke up. The operating system is the program that runs the machine itself, deciding which programs get the clerk, the desk, and the cabinet, and when. When you run two apps at once, it is the operating system that shares the clerk between them, a slice of ticks for this one, a slice for that one, so fast that both seem to run together. When an app asks to save a file, it asks the operating system, which owns the cabinet. When you tap and type, the operating system carries your input to the right program. Names you know, like Android and iOS and Windows, are operating systems. They are programs, written by people, made of instructions, fetched and executed by the same clerk who runs everything else. The machine is programs, managing programs, running programs, all the way down to the clerk and his three steps. There is no magic layer at the bottom. There is a very fast clerk, doing exactly what he is told, and the telling is very, very well organised.

This is your guided moment, and it is the same exercise the professionals do, at kitchen-table scale. Take the worked example and change one thing. Our program added a list of prices. Now, in plain words only, write the algorithm for a program that finds the biggest price in a list instead of the total. Do not write code. Write the method, the way the recipe was written. Keep a named place called biggest. Start it at the first price. Take each remaining price in turn. If a price is bigger than what is in biggest, replace what is in biggest with that price. When the list runs out, biggest is the answer. Now check your own algorithm the way the clerk would. Does it say what to do with the very first price? Does it say when to stop? Does it handle a list of one price, or an empty list? If you found yourself adding small clarifying sentences, you have just felt the real texture of programming. The method is easy to say. The method, said completely, with no gaps for the literal clerk to fall into, is the work. And it is learnable work, step by step, which is why this course teaches it the way it does.

Now the shadow side, honestly faced, because no lesson on programs is complete without it. Programs contain mistakes. A bug is a mistake in the instructions, a place where the program says something other than what its writer meant. Sit with that definition, because it explains the behaviour of every misbehaving machine you have ever met. The clerk is not malfunctioning when a bug bites. He is executing the buggy instruction with perfect fidelity, three billion times a second. The total comes out wrong because instruction four added the wrong box. The app closes suddenly because an instruction sent the clerk to a pigeonhole that held a letter code instead of an instruction, and he faithfully tried to obey a piece of text. Finding and fixing bugs is called debugging, and it is a large share of every programmer's working life, not because programmers are careless, but because programs are long, and a program of a million instructions offers a million places for a gap between what was meant and what was said. The lesson two saying applies here in its strongest form. Garbage in, garbage out. The clerk amplifies the program, wisdom or folly, exactly as written.

Let me tie this lesson back to the worked answer from lesson one, because the course is one building and you should see the beams connect. In lesson one I said a word processor is counting, plus four additions, wearing a friendly face. Representation, so the numbers can stand for letters. Stored instructions, which is today's lesson, the program kept as data the machine can fetch. Conditional branching, so the machine can test and choose. And input and output, so the world can reach the counting and the counting can reach the world. Now you can see the word processor with new eyes. When you type a letter, input carries the key press to the program. The program, an enormous descendant of our seven-instruction example, looks up the letter's number, stores it in memory among the other letters of your document, in variables and lists of variables. When you ask it to count your words, a loop walks the document exactly the way our loop walked the prices, testing each character, adding to a total. When you press save, the operating system carries the document from the desk to the cabinet, as lesson three described. When the program checks your spelling, it compares your words against a stored list, comparison being one of the clerk's oldest jobs. There is nothing in that application that is not built from the pieces on this table. The pieces are few. The arrangements are vast. That is the whole aesthetic of computing, and once you see it, you cannot unsee it, in any program, on any machine, for the rest of your life.

A word about size, to keep your sense of scale honest. Our worked program had 7 instructions. A small phone app might have a million instructions. The operating system beneath it has tens of millions. These numbers are not written by one person typing quickly. They are written by teams, over years, reusing pieces other teams wrote, the way a house is built from bricks nobody on the site fired themselves. Programs that other programmers can reuse as building blocks are called libraries, and modern programming is largely the art of choosing good blocks and writing the comparatively small amount of new instruction that makes this app different from every other app. When an app on your phone updates and the notes say bug fixes, you now know precisely what happened. Someone found places where the instructions said something other than what was meant, corrected the writing, translated it again, and sent the new instructions to your cabinet. The clerk noticed nothing. He simply began fetching a better set of orders.

And a word about trust, because it follows from everything today and it matters for your business and your life. A program does what its instructions say, and its instructions were written by people you will never meet, working for companies with their own interests. The clerk cannot protect you from a program that was written to take more than it should, any more than he can protect you from an honest mistake. He obeys both with the same fidelity. That is why later lessons in this path, and the lessons of your own experience, will keep returning to a simple discipline. Know what program you are running. Know who wrote it. Know what it asks for. The machine's faithfulness is a fact. What the machine is being faithful to is a choice, and the choice is made by people, which means it can be examined by people, including you.

One more building block before the recap, because without it the vast arrangements I keep mentioning would collapse under their own size. Imagine writing out the full instructions for adding a list of prices every single time any program needed a total. Then writing them again for the next program, and the next, thousands of times, with a fresh chance for a bug in every copy. No sane craft works that way, and programming does not either. Instead, a useful set of instructions is written once, given a name, and kept ready. A function is a named set of instructions that does one job and can be used again and again, wherever that job is needed. Our price-adding loop, wrapped up and named total, becomes a function. A program that needs a total does not rewrite the loop. It calls the function, hands it a list, and receives the answer, the way you hand a trusted worker a stack of invoices and receive a total. Functions can be built out of other functions, the way our total could be used by a larger function that prepares a whole bill, adding the prices, then adding tax, then formatting the result for the customer. Programs within programs, instructions calling instructions, each layer standing on the one below. That is the honest meaning of the title of this lesson. It is instructions, arranged in layers, all the way down, until at the very bottom the layers run out and there is only the clerk, his three steps, and the numbers. Every layer is somebody's writing. Every layer can be read, checked, and fixed by somebody who knows how. There is no layer where the magic lives and the explaining stops.

This layering is also why a person can learn to program in stages, and why this course is ordered the way it is. You do not need to hold a million instructions in your head, any more than a builder holds a whole house in his hands at once. You hold one function, one job, clearly. You test it the way we traced the little program, with numbers whose answers you already know. Then you trust it, the way you trust a finished wall, and you build on top of it. The professionals who write the programs your business runs on work exactly this way, one clear layer at a time, and the distance between their work and the trace you did today is a distance of practice and scale, not of kind. I want you to remember that. The clerk does not know whether he is running seven instructions or seventy million. He fetches, he decodes, he executes, and the layers above him, built by patient people out of small clear pieces, are what turn that simple faithfulness into a working world.

And one short story, because this class learns from stories as well as from definitions, and this one is true to the way the work feels. A programmer writes a program late at night. She traces it in her head the way we traced ours, and it works on paper. She runs it, and the total comes out wrong, not wildly wrong, just wrong by the price of the first item, every time. The clerk is not broken. The program has a gap exactly where lesson two said gaps live. Her loop tests whether the position has reached the end before it adds, and her starting position skips the first price entirely. The fix is two instructions changing places. Two instructions, in a program she wrote in an hour, and the hunt for them took longer than the writing. I tell you this so that when a program of yours, or a program you paid for, misbehaves in some small stubborn way, you will picture the truth of it. Somewhere in a long list of faithful instructions, one or two are saying something slightly different from what their writer meant, and a person with patience and a worked example can find them. That is debugging, from the inside, and it is ordinary, honourable work, not a sign that the machine is haunted or that the writer was a fool.

Let us recap, in order. First, a program is a set of instructions stored in memory, written in advance, that the processor fetches and follows one by one. Second, the stored program idea means instructions are data, kept in the same memory as numbers, which is why one machine can become a camera, a map, or an office just by loading different instructions. Third, an algorithm is a method for solving a problem, written as a clear sequence of steps that always finishes and always gives the answer. Fourth, a variable is a named place in memory that holds a value, and the value can change as the program runs. Fifth, people write programs in programming languages, and a translator program turns that writing into machine code, either all at once beforehand, which is a compiler, or piece by piece while it runs, which is an interpreter. Sixth, the operating system is the program that runs the machine itself, sharing the clerk, the desk, and the cabinet among all the other programs. And seventh, a bug is a mistake in the instructions, a place where the program says something other than what its writer meant, and debugging is the work of finding and fixing those places.

Next lesson, lesson five, the machines stop working alone. Networks, computers talking to each other, and what can go wrong when they do. Everything you have built, the bits, the clerk, the desk, the programs, is about to be connected to every other machine on Earth, and the consequences, good and bad, are the world you live in now.

First, your questions on this lesson. They cover the program, the algorithm, the translation, and the worked example with the prices, and nothing I did not teach. You have earned these questions, because you have done the real work of the lesson already, tracing a program by hand and writing an algorithm of your own. Answer them in that same spirit, slowly and exactly, and when a question names a definition, give the definition the way the lesson gave it, in plain words you understand. The full text stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. If a question sends you back to the trace of the little program, walk it again with your finger on the instructions, the way we did together. That trace is the heart of the lesson, and it is worth the walk. I will see you in lesson five.

lessons.title: Networks: computers talking, and what can go wrong
paragraphs: Welcome back. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations. This is lesson five, and its title is Networks: computers talking, and what can go wrong. For four lessons, our computer has been alone. A brilliant clerk, a desk, a filing cabinet, programs written in advance, all of it inside one box. But the computer in your pocket is almost never alone, and it is not very interesting alone. Its photographs travel to other machines. Its messages arrive from across oceans. Its programs consult computers in buildings you will never see, in towns you cannot name. Today the machines start talking to each other, and by the end of this lesson you will know what a network is, how a message actually crosses the world, why it travels in small pieces with addresses on them, and the honest list of what can go wrong along the way, including the part where strangers try to listen in, and what honest people do about that.

The definition first, as always, plain and keepable. A network is a set of computers connected so that they can exchange data, pass messages, and share what they have. Two computers and a connection is a network, the smallest one there is. Your phone and your laptop, sharing a photograph across your kitchen, are a network at work. The internet, which we will come to properly, is the largest network, built by joining millions of smaller networks together until the whole planet is one conversation. The connection itself can be a wire, carrying electricity, or a glass fibre, carrying light, or open air, carrying radio waves, which is what Wi-Fi is. Wi-Fi is simply a network connection made by radio instead of by wire. The clerk does not care which it is. Bits are bits, and a bit that arrives by radio is worth exactly as much as a bit that arrives by copper.

Now, how does a message actually travel? Here is where most people's picture is wrong, so let me replace it with the right one. The wrong picture is a pipe, one continuous stream flowing from your phone to your friend's phone, the way water flows through a hose. The right picture is the postal service. When you send a photograph to a friend, the photograph does not travel whole. It is broken into small pieces, each piece is put in its own envelope with an address on it, the envelopes travel by whatever routes are open, some fast, some slow, some by different roads entirely, and at the far end the envelopes are gathered, checked, and opened in the right order, and the photograph is rebuilt. If that sounds inefficient, hold your judgment. By the end of this section you will see it is one of the smartest designs in all of computing.

The pieces have a name. A packet is a small piece of a message, travelling with the address of where it is going and a note of where it belongs in the whole. Every word of that matters. Small piece, because small pieces are easy to move, easy to resend, and easy to share a road with. The address of where it is going, because the road is shared by billions of envelopes and each one must be directable on its own. And a note of where it belongs in the whole, a sequence number, because envelopes that travel different roads arrive out of order, and the receiver must be able to lay them back in sequence, envelope twelve after envelope eleven, before opening them.

How small is small? A typical packet carries about 1500 bytes of actual message, plus its addressing. Now let us count, the way this class counts, in a worked example you can check. Suppose you send a photograph that takes up 3 megabytes. In strict bundles, that is 3145728 bytes. Divide by the 1500 bytes each packet can carry. 3145728 divided by 1500 is about 2097. Your one photograph crosses the world as roughly 2097 separate packets, each with the same destination address, each with its own sequence number, travelling independently, and your friend's phone rebuilds the picture from the pile. When the picture appears on her screen a second later, whole and perfect, that rebuilding is part of what just happened, invisibly, at machine speed. I never stop finding that wonderful. A photograph, shredded into two thousand envelopes, thrown onto a shared planetary road system, and reassembled without a single piece out of place, as a routine event, billions of times a day.

The address on each packet deserves its own attention, because addresses are where networks become a system instead of a tangle. Every machine on a network has an address, a number that identifies it, the way a house has a number on its street. On the internet, the classic form of the address is 4 numbers separated by dots, each number between zero and two hundred and fifty-five. You will recognise that range. Zero to two hundred and fifty-five is exactly one byte's worth of values, lesson one's byte, so the classic internet address is 4 bytes long, one byte per number. That address is called an IP address, and IP stands for Internet Protocol, a name you are about to meet again. When your phone sends a packet, it writes two addresses on the envelope. Its own address, so the answer can find its way back, and the destination's address, so the packet can find its way there. A packet without both is a letter with no destination and no return address, and the network treats it the way you would. It goes nowhere useful.

Who reads the addresses and moves the packets along? Machines called routers. A router is a computer whose whole job is to receive packets, read their destination addresses, and send them onward along the best available road toward that destination. Picture a sorting office that never sleeps and sorts at the speed of light. Your packet will usually pass through several routers on its journey, each one making one decision. Not the whole route. Just the next hop, the next office closer to the destination. This is a profound design choice, and it is why the internet can be so large. No single machine needs to know the whole map. Each router knows its neighbours and a sense of direction, the way you can cross a country by following signs town by town without holding the whole road atlas in your head at once. Local knowledge, faithfully applied, packet by packet, produces a global result. You have seen that pattern before in this course. Simple steps, arranged well, at enormous scale. It is the clerk's philosophy, grown up into a planet.

For any of this to work between machines built by different companies, in different countries, in different decades, the talking itself must follow agreed rules. You have met this idea twice already, as the codes of lesson one. Here it grows up and gets its grown-up name. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for how computers talk, so that a machine built by one company can understand a machine built by another. Protocols decide everything about the conversation. How a conversation starts. How packets are addressed. How the receiver says, I got that one, send the next. How errors are reported. How the conversation ends. The Internet Protocol, the IP in the address, is the protocol that handles addressing and routing, the envelope system itself. Its usual partner is the protocol that handles reliability, checking that every packet arrived and asking for the missing ones again, and its initials are TCP. When people say TCP/IP, they are naming the pair of agreements the whole internet runs on, the envelope rules and the delivery-checking rules together. Nobody owns these agreements. They are published, public, and free for anyone to follow, which is precisely why everyone did, and why a phone built this year can talk to a machine built before its owner was born.

Two more roles, and then we can trace a whole conversation. When your phone asks for something, a web page, your messages, a map, it is playing the role called the client. The client is the machine that asks. The machine that answers has the other famous name. A server is a computer that waits for requests and answers them, serving programs, pages, and files to the machines that ask. A server is not a different species of machine. It is an ordinary computer, usually a powerful one in a building full of its colleagues, running a program whose whole job is to wait politely, listen for requests, and respond. Your messages live on servers. When a friend sends you a message and your phone is off, the message waits on a server, patient as a clerk with a pigeonhole, until your phone wakes and asks for it. That is why the message arrives the moment you switch on. It was never travelling all that time. It was being served, held ready by a machine whose job is holding things ready.

And a distinction that will keep you clear-headed for years. The internet and the web are not the same thing. The internet is the network itself, the roads, the envelopes, the sorting offices, the whole planetary system for moving packets. The web is one famous use of those roads, the system of pages and links you visit with a browser. Your email also rides the internet, and your messages, and your video calls, and none of those are the web. The web is a city. The internet is the road network the city is built on, and other cities use the same roads. People who confuse the two end up confused about everything built on them, and you will not be one of those people.

This is your guided moment, and it is a trace, the way we traced the little program in lesson four. Trace one message with me, from your phone to a friend's phone, naming each stage out loud. Stage one. You type the message and press send. Your phone's program turns the letters into numbers, lesson one, and breaks the numbers into packets, each with your address and your friend's address, or rather the address of the server that serves your friend, written on it. Stage two. The packets leave your phone by radio, Wi-Fi or the mobile network, to the first router they meet. Stage three. Router by router, hop by hop, each reading only the destination and choosing the next road, the packets cross whatever distance separates you, under streets and, if your friend is far away, under an ocean, as light in glass fibres. Stage four. The server receives the packets, checks them against their sequence numbers, asks again for any that went missing, and rebuilds your message whole. Stage five. Your friend's phone, asking politely as a client does, receives the message from the server and rebuilds it on its desk, and the letters appear. Five stages, and every technology in this lesson appears in the trace exactly once, doing its own job. If you can retell that trace without me, you understand how the internet works at the level most of its users never reach. Try it once more in your head before we move on. Phone, router, roads, server, phone.

Now the second half of the title, faced squarely. What can go wrong? The honest list, in order of ordinariness. Packets get lost. A router is overwhelmed, a road is cut, a radio signal fades at the wrong moment, and an envelope simply never arrives. This is so ordinary that the system is built expecting it. The checking protocol notices the gap in the sequence numbers, and the receiver asks for that packet again, and the sender sends another copy. You never see it happen. You only see its cost, the slight delay while a video stutters or a page hesitates. Roads get crowded. When too many packets want the same road at the same moment, they queue, and everything slows, the way traffic slows, and for the same reason. That crowding is called congestion, and the delay it causes, the time a packet spends travelling and queuing, is called latency. A connection can have enormous capacity and still feel slow if its latency is high, the way a wide highway with a two-hour jam moves many cars and pleases none of them. Addresses get confused, or machines go away. The server you are asking may be switched off, broken, or simply gone, and your request travels faithfully to a door nobody answers. And cables get cut, storms take down radio towers, and whole regions can fall quiet for a while. The network's great strength is that it was designed for exactly this world. Many roads, independent packets, local decisions. Cut one road and the routers, faithful clerks that they are, simply start choosing the next best road, and the conversation flows around the damage like water around a stone.

But there is a darker item on the list of what can go wrong, and a foundations course that skipped it would be failing you. Packets travel through machines owned by strangers. A letter in the post can be steamed open. A packet can be copied as it passes, and neither sender nor receiver would ever know. On an open network, anything you send can, in principle, be read by someone it was never meant for, and some of what you send is worth reading. Passwords. Bank details. Private messages. Business numbers. So the network's users developed the same answer the letter-writers developed centuries ago, improved by mathematics. Sealed envelopes, of a very strong kind.

The sealing is called encryption. Encryption is scrambling a message with a secret key so that anyone who intercepts it sees only nonsense, and only the intended reader can unscramble it. A key, here, is a secret number, held by the people who are allowed to read. The scrambling is not a simple shuffle. It is arithmetic, done by programs, using the clerk's own operations at enormous scale, arranged so that unscrambling without the key would take longer than anyone can wait, while unscrambling with the key is instant. When you see a small padlock sign beside a web address, it means the conversation between your machine and that server is encrypted. The packets still travel the shared roads. Strangers can still copy them as they pass. What they copy is nonsense to them, and that nonsense is the whole point. Your business can cross a planet of strangers' machines and remain your business. In lesson four I told you the clerk obeys any program faithfully, including a dishonest one. Encryption is the other side of that coin. Faithful arithmetic, arranged by honest people, standing guard over everything you send.

The remaining danger is not technical at all, and it is the one that harms the most people. The network carries messages from anyone, including people who lie about who they are. A message can claim to be from your bank and be from a thief. A page can wear the colours of a company you trust and belong to a stranger. This trick has a name, phishing, which is fishing with a lure, and the lure is your trust. No protocol can fully protect you, because the attack is not on the machines. It is on the reader. The defences are habits, and they belong in a foundations course, so here they are, plainly. Be suspicious of urgency, because honest institutions rarely demand instant action by message. Check where a message actually came from and where its links actually lead, not where they claim to lead. And remember lesson four's discipline, which now covers the whole network. Know what program you are running, know who you are really talking to, and treat a request for your password or your money arriving out of the blue as a lure until it proves otherwise. The clerk cannot smell a lie. You can learn to. That is a human job, and it stays human.

One more piece of honest arithmetic before the recap, because network speeds are advertised at everyone and understood by few. A connection's speed is measured in bits per second, how many bits the road can carry each second. A typical home connection might offer 100 megabits per second, one hundred million bits streaming past. Notice the unit. Bits, not bytes. Advertisements count in bits because the number is eight times bigger, and now you know a byte is 8 bits, so you can translate for yourself. A file of 100 megabytes is 800 megabits of travelling, and on a perfect 100 megabit connection it would take 8 seconds to arrive. Divide the file, counted in bits, by the road, counted in bits per second, and you have the seconds. Real roads are never perfect, so real times are longer, but the arithmetic gives you the floor, and a person who can compute the floor cannot be fooled by the ceiling painted on the box.

Wait. A careful student has spotted a gap, and I want to honour it before the recap. I told you every machine has a number for an address, and packets travel by numbers. But you do not type numbers when you visit a website or open an app. You use names. Names are for people. Numbers are for machines. Something must translate between them, every time, invisibly, and that something is one of the hardest-working agreements on the internet. The Domain Name System is the internet's phone book, a vast distributed directory that translates the names people remember into the numbers machines use. When you ask for a site by name, your machine first consults this directory, receives the number belonging to that name, and only then writes its packets, because packets cannot be addressed to a name any more than a letter can be delivered to a nickname. The directory is distributed, meaning there is no single phone book in one building that the world depends on. Copies and partial copies live on servers everywhere, asking each other, caching answers, updating constantly. If the directory fails, the roads are still there and the machines are still there, but nobody can find anybody, which is why a certain kind of internet failure feels so strange. Nothing is broken, and nothing can be reached. You now know enough to diagnose that feeling. The names stopped resolving into numbers.

Your own home sits inside this picture in a way worth seeing once, clearly. The box your provider gave you, the one with the blinking lights, is doing three of this lesson's jobs at once. It is a router, sorting packets between your machines and the world. It runs your Wi-Fi, the radio connection your phone joins. And it gives each of your machines a local address, so the printer, the laptop, and the phone can find each other across the kitchen without troubling the planet. When the connection at home fails and someone tells you to turn the box off and on again, you can now translate that advice into clerk language. You are restarting a small, faithful computer whose programs have got themselves into a state their writers did not intend, and a fresh start hands it clean instructions and an empty desk. It works for the same reason it worked in lesson two. The clerk was never broken. He was trapped, and you have freed him.

And notice, as we stand back, what the network has done to the meaning of the word computer. In lesson one, a computer was a box that counts. By lesson four, it was a box that counts, remembers, and follows programs. Now the box is a doorway. The programs it runs reach across the world as a matter of routine. The files it opens may live on another continent. The friend it talks to is a machine in a rack in a building with no sign on it. Nothing about the clerk changed. He still fetches, decodes, and executes, three billion times a second, in the phone in your hand. What changed is the reach of his errands. His instructions now routinely say, ask a machine across the ocean, and wait for its answer, and the waiting, which lesson three taught you to respect, is measured in the latency of roads and the patience of servers. The whole modern world is that sentence, running at scale. You understand it now from the bit upward, and very few people on Earth can honestly say that.

One more ordinary miracle deserves a sentence before we close, because you use it every day and it gathers the whole lesson into one gesture. A video call. Your voice is measured thousands of times a second and turned into numbers, lesson one's representation, working on sound. The numbers are broken into packets, addressed, and sent hop by hop across the roads, and here the design shows its judgement, because for a live voice a late packet is a useless packet. There is no time to ask for it again. So the call does not ask. It lets the missing sliver of sound go, covers the gap as gracefully as it can, and keeps the conversation in the present moment, which is why a bad connection makes a voice crackle and drop syllables instead of pausing to repair itself. Email makes the opposite choice. A missing packet in a message is worth waiting for, so the checking protocol asks, and asks again, until every envelope has arrived. Same roads, same packets, two different bargains with loss, chosen by the programs to fit the job. When you know that, the behaviour of your own machines stops being weather and becomes engineering, visible and understandable, and that change, from weather to engineering, is the real product of this entire course. Hold onto that thought when your own connection next misbehaves in the middle of something that matters. Instead of shaking the phone, you will find yourself asking the engineer's questions. Is it the road, the address, the server, or the crowd? Four suspects, and this lesson has taught you how each one behaves and how each one announces itself.

Let us recap, in order. First, a network is a set of computers connected so that they can exchange data, pass messages, and share what they have. Second, messages do not travel whole. They are broken into packets, and a packet is a small piece of a message, travelling with the address of where it is going and a note of where it belongs in the whole. Third, every machine has an address, the classic internet address being 4 numbers, each one byte's worth, from zero to two hundred and fifty-five. Fourth, routers are the sorting offices, reading each packet's destination and choosing the next hop, needing only local knowledge to produce a global result. Fifth, a protocol is an agreed set of rules for how computers talk, and the internet runs on such agreements, addressing and routing in one, delivery-checking in the other. Sixth, the machine that asks is the client, and a server is a computer that waits for requests and answers them. Seventh, the internet is the road system, and the web is only one city built on it. And eighth, what can go wrong is a real list. Packets are lost and resent, roads congest and latency grows, machines go silent, strangers listen, which encryption answers by scrambling, and liars send lures, which only your own habits answer.

Next lesson, lesson six, the final lesson of this course, brings everything home. Files, formats, and where your data actually lives. What a file really is, why the same photograph can be a different size in a different format, and the truthful answer, in several places at once, to the question of where your pictures and your business records are sitting right now.

First, your questions on this lesson. They cover the packets, the addresses, the roles, and the dangers, and nothing I did not teach. Take them at the pace of the sorting office, one envelope at a time, and do not be discouraged if the danger questions feel heavier than the others. They are meant to be answered slowly, from the lesson, with the habits it taught you held firmly in mind. The full text stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. The trace of the message, phone to router to roads to server to phone, is the spine of the lesson. If a question troubles you, walk the trace again and see where its answer lives along the road. You have come a long way from counting on your fingers, and the distance was covered entirely with ideas you can now say in your own words. I will see you in lesson six.

lessons.title: Files, formats, and where your data actually lives
paragraphs: Welcome back. In this room, AI and Computing is learned by doing it, not by watching it. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and this is Computing Foundations. This is lesson six, the final lesson of the course, and its title is Files, formats, and where your data actually lives. You have built the whole machine now. Bits and bytes. The clerk and his three steps. The desk and the filing cabinet. Programs, instructions all the way down. Networks, packets crossing the planet. Today we finish with the thing you actually touch every day, the file. The photograph. The document. The song. The spreadsheet with your business numbers in it. By the end of this lesson you will know what a file really is, why the same photograph can be a huge file or a small one depending on its format, what people are truly saying when they say your data is in the cloud, and how many places your most important photograph is sitting in right now. That last answer surprises almost everyone, and it matters, because some of those places are safer than you think and one of them is less safe than you hope.

The definition first, one last time, plain and keepable. A file is a named collection of bytes, kept in storage, that a program can open, read, and write as one thing. Unpack it. A collection of bytes. Underneath the icon and the friendly name, a file is bytes, lesson one's bytes, numbers in rows, nothing else. Named. The name is how you and the machine refer to the collection as a whole, instead of pointing at a stretch of the cabinet. Kept in storage. Files live in the cabinet, lesson three's cabinet, because files are for keeping, and the desk is only where a file is worked on while a program has it open. And the last clause is the soul of it. A program can open, read, and write it as one thing. When you open a photograph, you do not fetch its millions of bytes one by one. You name the file, and the operating system hands the whole collection to the program as a single object. The file is the unit of keeping, the way the byte is the unit of counting and the packet is the unit of travelling. Everything you own, digitally speaking, you own as files.

The name itself teaches more than people realise, so let us look at one closely. A file's name usually comes in two parts, joined by a dot. The first part is the name you chose, the human part, like a label on a folder that says what is inside. The second part, after the dot, is called the extension, and it is a short code, usually three or four letters, that announces the file's format. You have seen them all your life. A name ending in the letters for a text file. A photograph ending in the letters of its picture format. A document ending in the letters of the program family that made it. The extension is a promise, made by whoever wrote the file, about how the bytes inside are arranged. And that word, format, is the second great idea of this lesson, so here is its definition, and keep it next to the first. A format is the agreement that says how the bytes inside a file are arranged, so that a program opening the file knows what the numbers mean.

You should feel a click of recognition there, because a format is lesson one's representation, grown up and given a filing system. Representation said, numbers stand for letters and colours by agreed codes. A format is the whole agreement, written down, for one kind of thing. The format for a plain text file says, these bytes are numbers for characters, one after another, in this code, and nothing else is hidden in here. The format for a common kind of photograph says, these first bytes describe the picture's width and height, and the rest are compressed colour information, arranged in this exact pattern, to be rebuilt by this exact method. A program that knows the format can open the file and make sense of it. A program that does not know the format sees only numbers with no agreement attached, a book in a language it cannot read. This is why a file can be perfectly intact and perfectly useless at the same time. The bytes survived. The agreement is missing. When a customer sends your business a file your programs cannot open, nothing is broken and nothing is lost. You are simply holding numbers whose arrangement nobody on your machine has been told. The cure is a program that knows that format, and now you understand the cure instead of just hoping for it.

Now the question everyone asks about photographs, answered properly. Why is one photograph a small file and another, of what looks like the same scene, an enormous one? Three reasons, and you have the tools for all three. First, the count of pixels. A modern phone camera captures a picture of perhaps 4000 pixels wide by 3000 pixels tall. Multiply, the way we multiply in this class. 4000 times 3000 is 12000000 pixels, twelve million dots, each one needing its colour stored. Second, the bytes per pixel. Lesson one taught you a pixel's colour is three numbers, three bytes, one each for red, green, and blue. Twelve million pixels at three bytes each is 36000000 bytes, thirty-six megabytes, for the raw picture with nothing clever done to it. Third, and this is where the format earns its keep, compression. Compression is the art of describing the same thing with fewer bytes, by finding patterns in the numbers and writing the patterns instead. A photograph of a blue sky has thousands of neighbouring pixels that are nearly the same blue. The raw format writes that blue out in full, thousands of times. A compressing format writes, in effect, this blue, repeated across this whole stretch, and moves on. The common photograph format on phones does this kind of work aggressively and well, and it brings our thirty-six megabyte picture down to about 3 megabytes, roughly a twelfth of the raw size, small enough to send as those two thousand packets from lesson five. Same camera. Same scene. The file's size is mostly a story about how cleverly its format describes patterns, and now you can read that story.

Compression has a fork in it, and an honest course names both branches. Some compression is lossless, which means the original numbers can be rebuilt exactly, every last bit, from the compressed file. Nothing is thrown away. The patterns are merely described more cleverly. Text files and business documents are compressed this way when they are compressed at all, because a contract that comes back almost identical is not identical, and almost is not good enough for words and numbers that carry money. Other compression is lossy, which means some of the original numbers are thrown away on purpose, because a program has judged that your eye or your ear will not miss them. The photograph format on your phone is lossy. It keeps the patterns your eye is sensitive to and quietly discards fine detail your eye would never have caught, and in exchange it gives you that twelvefold saving. Lossy is not cheating. It is a bargain, openly made, detail traded for size, and for photographs of birthdays and finished jobs it is a bargain worth making every time. But know which bargain a file has made. A lossy copy can never be turned back into the original, because the discarded numbers are gone. If a file is the only record of something that matters, the original, uncompressed or losslessly kept, is the one your cabinet should hold.

A file also carries a quiet passenger, and it explains a small mystery you may have wondered about. Alongside the main content, many formats store metadata, which means data about the data. A photograph's file commonly records when it was taken, what camera took it, its dimensions, and often where on Earth it was taken, written there by the phone's sense of its own location. That is how your photo app can show you a map of your pictures, and sort them by the day, without you ever typing a word. The file told it. Metadata is useful, and it is also worth knowing about with clear eyes, because a photograph you send to a stranger may carry the location of your home or your business inside it, in numbers you never see on the screen. Lesson five taught you to think about who can read what you send. Metadata is part of that thinking. The file is never only the picture. It is the picture, plus its papers.

Now, organisation, briefly, because a cabinet without order is a pile. Files are grouped into folders, which are named collections of files, and folders can sit inside folders, the way a cabinet has drawers and each drawer has dividers. Every file therefore has not just a name but a place, and the full description of its place, folder inside folder inside folder, is called its path. When a program cannot find a file, it is usually the path that is wrong, not the file. The file is sitting exactly where it was put. The directions were wrong. And deleting, since we are being honest about everything today, deserves its sentence. When you delete a file, the machine mostly removes its name and its place from the cabinet's index and marks the space as free. The bytes themselves often linger for a while, until new files are written over them. Deleting is closer to tearing the label off a folder and pencilling the shelf as empty than it is to burning the contents. That is why deleted files can sometimes be recovered, and why a machine being sold or given away deserves more than a quick delete of the things you cared about. The cabinet remembers more than its index admits.

And now the title's final question, the one I promised would surprise you. Where does your data actually live? Start with the answer you already know. A file you saved lives in the storage of the machine you saved it on, in flash chips in your phone, on the drive in your laptop. That is place one, and for an older way of computing it was the only place. But your phone is almost certainly doing something else as well, quietly, in the background, over the network from lesson five. It is copying your files to servers owned by the company whose services you use, and those copies are what people mean by the cloud. So let us say it with total plainness, because this sentence dissolves a decade of fog. The cloud is other people's servers, computers in data centres, rented out as storage and programs that your machine reaches over the network. There is no sky involved. There are buildings, full of servers, with power and cooling and staff, in particular places under particular laws, and your photographs are on their drives. That is not a reason for alarm. Those buildings are usually far better guarded, powered, and backed up than any phone in any pocket. But it is a reason for clear thinking. A file in the cloud lives in two kinds of place at once, your cabinet and theirs, under your account, reachable by your password, which is why lesson five's habits about passwords and lures guard your files as surely as any lock guards a drawer.

The copying has a name of its own. When your phone and the cloud keep the same file in step, so that a photograph taken in the morning is on the server by the time you sit down, and a document edited on the laptop appears on the phone, that keeping-in-step is called synchronisation, or sync for short. Sync is a program, of course, lesson four's programs again, watching for changes and sending packets, lesson five's packets, carrying the changed bytes to the other copies. Sync is why your data feels like it lives everywhere. It does live in several places, and the places are kept in agreement by tireless, literal programs doing exactly what they were told.

Which brings us to the most practical idea in the entire course, and I have saved it for last on purpose, because you now have everything needed to understand why it is true. A backup is a second copy of a file, kept in a different place from the first, made so that losing the first copy is an inconvenience instead of a disaster. Read the middle of that definition again. In a different place. A second copy on the same phone is not a backup against the phone being lost, because both copies go in the same moment. A copy in the cloud is a genuine second place, which is the cloud's deepest virtue, deeper than convenience. And here is the rule that follows, and I give it to you as the working law of this whole subject. If a file exists in only one place, it is one accident away from not existing at all. Phones are dropped in lakes. Cabinets fail without warning. Buildings, even good ones, have bad days. The files that survive history, the photographs your grandchildren will hold, the records your business stands on, are the files that lived in more than one place when the accident came. Count your copies of anything that matters. If the count is one, you do not have a keeping problem tomorrow. You have one today, and it is fixable today, cheaply, with the tools already in your pocket.

This is your guided moment, the last one of the course, and it gathers the whole lesson into one honest inventory. Take one photograph that matters to you, the one you would rescue first. Now count its homes, out loud, one by one. It lives in your phone's storage, in the flash chips, as a lossy compressed file in the phone's photograph format. That is one. If your phone syncs, it lives again on a server in a data centre, in the same format, under your account. That is two. If you sent it to someone you love, it lives on their phone as well, and probably in their cloud too. That is three, and four. If it appears in a message thread, the messaging service's servers hold their own copy. The count grows quickly, and notice the two lessons hiding in it. Your data is harder to lose than you feared, because it has quietly become a small crowd of copies. And your data is in more hands than you remembered, because every copy is a place, and every place has keepers. Both lessons are the same lesson, seen from two sides. Data lives in places, places are physical, and a person who knows the places can make clear-eyed decisions about all of it. You are now such a person.

Let me also close the loop with lesson one's worked answer, one final time, because a course should end where it began, with the student seeing the starting problem with new eyes. The set problem asked what has to be added to counting before you get a word processor. Counting. Representation. Stored instructions. Conditional branching. Input and output. You have now studied every one of those from the inside. You know counting is binary and lives in bytes. You know representation grows up into formats, whole agreements about what numbers mean. You know stored instructions are programs, and programs are instructions all the way down to a faithful clerk. You know branching is a single bit steering a machine. You know input and output became, in lesson five, a conversation with the whole planet. The word processor on your screen is not a mystery wearing a friendly face anymore. It is a construction you can describe, layer by layer, in plain language, and defend every claim you make about it. That was the promise of this course, made in lesson one, and it is kept.

Before the recap, let me give you one more worked example, small and complete, because file sizes for words behave very differently from file sizes for pictures, and the difference is worth feeling in numbers. Take a full page of writing, a long letter to a customer. A page holds roughly 2000 characters, letters, spaces, and punctuation together. In a plain text format, each character is one byte, lesson one's agreement, one number per letter. So the whole page, the whole letter, is about 2000 bytes, two kilobytes, for everything on it. Now compare the photograph we counted earlier, three megabytes after compression. Three megabytes is 3000 kilobytes. Your photograph weighs as much as 1500 pages of writing. Fifteen hundred letters to customers, or one picture of the finished job. That is why your cabinet fills with photographs and videos while a lifetime of documents barely makes a dent, and why the businesses that drown in storage costs are always drowning in images, never in words. Words are nearly free to keep. Pictures are the heavy furniture. When you plan where your business files will live, plan around the furniture.

The same arithmetic, turned around, is quietly hopeful for your records. A lifetime of invoices, contracts, and customer lists, kept as documents, is a rounding error in a modern cabinet. There is no storage excuse for keeping only one copy of them, and after today's lesson there is no knowledge excuse either. The copies cost almost nothing. The loss, if it comes, costs whatever the records were worth, which for a business can be everything. I do not teach this as fear. I teach it as arithmetic. Small numbers on one side, large numbers on the other, and a decision that makes itself once both sides are on the table where you can see them. That, in the end, is what this whole course has been training. Not fear of the machine, and not worship of it either. Clear numbers, plain definitions, and decisions that make themselves.

One last distinction, drawn the way I like distinctions drawn, between two words people use as if they were twins. Saving and backing up are not the same act. Saving, from lesson three, is the walk from the desk to the cabinet of the same machine. It protects your work from the power going. Backing up is a copy arriving in a different place entirely, another machine, another building, another keeper. It protects your work from the machine going. A man can save faithfully every hour of his life and still lose everything in one bad minute, because all his saving happened inside a single cabinet. And a man can back up once, years ago, and lose everything since, because the copies were never kept in step. The complete habit is both, saving as you work and copies flowing to a second place as you go, and the beautiful fact of modern machines is that both can be made automatic, done by programs, while you think about your actual work. Set it once, with clear eyes, knowing exactly what each copy is and where it sleeps. Then get on with your life, in a house where the records can survive the accidents. That is the practical summit of this course, and it is entirely within your reach tonight.

And because this is the final lesson, allow me one paragraph of plain regard before the formality of the recap. You came to this course, if you came the way most of my students come, using these machines every day of your life while suspecting they were sealed boxes that other people understood and you merely operated. That suspicion is finished now. You have counted in binary on your own fingers. You have traced a clerk through his cycle and a program through its loop. You have watched a photograph become two thousand packets and become a photograph again, and you have counted the homes of a picture you love. None of that was done for you. You did it, in this room, by doing, which is the only way it has ever been learned. Whatever you build next, on this foundation or in the world outside it, will be built by someone who knows what is under the floorboards. I do not offer praise cheaply, and I do not offer it now cheaply. You have earned the foundation. Build on it.

There is one more habit of mind I want to leave installed, because it will keep working for you long after the details of any single lesson have settled. Whenever a machine, a salesperson, or a headline presents you with a wonder, ask the three questions this course has taught you to ask. What are the numbers underneath it, and can I count them? What are the instructions, and who wrote them? And where does the thing actually live, in which cabinet, in which building, under whose keeping? A wonder that survives those three questions is a tool you can use with confidence. A wonder that dissolves under them was fog, and fog is best identified before it is paid for. You have every tool those questions require. Bits, bytes, and bundles for the counting. The clerk and his programs for the instructions. The desk, the cabinet, the roads, and the data centres for the places. Keep the questions sharp and the machines will stay what they were always meant to be. Servants of the people who understand them, and you are one of those people now.

Let us recap this lesson, in order. First, a file is a named collection of bytes, kept in storage, that a program can open, read, and write as one thing. Second, the extension at the end of a file's name announces its format. Third, a format is the agreement that says how the bytes inside a file are arranged, so that a program opening the file knows what the numbers mean. Fourth, file size is a story of pixels, bytes per pixel, and compression, and compression is the art of describing the same thing with fewer bytes, lossless when nothing may be lost and lossy when detail is traded for size on purpose. Fifth, files carry metadata, data about the data, including when and often where a photograph was taken. Sixth, the cloud is other people's servers, computers in data centres, and sync is the program-driven copying that keeps your copies in step. And seventh, a backup is a second copy kept in a different place, and a file that exists in only one place is one accident away from not existing at all.

And the course itself, in one breath, because you have earned the whole view. Computers count with two fingers and build everything from one small choice. A literal clerk follows stored instructions at inhuman speed. A fast forgetful desk and a slow faithful cabinet divide the keeping between them. Programs turn methods into orders, and networks turn lone machines into a planet-wide conversation. Files are how it all becomes yours, named and formatted and copied into places you can count. Six lessons. One machine, understood. There is no part of the device in your pocket that is magic to you now, and that was the entire point.

What comes next, after these questions, is the rest of the path. The other classes in AI and Computing will take this foundation and build on it, how machines learn, how they act, what data proves and what it only pretends to prove. Every one of them assumes what you now know, and you do know it, in your hands and in your own words, not as phrases you memorised but as a machine you can describe.

First, your final questions. They cover the file, the format, the compression, and the places your data lives, and nothing I did not teach. Answer them the way you have answered in this room all along, from the lesson itself, in plain words, with the numbers worked honestly where numbers are asked for. There is no trick waiting in them and no shame in returning to the text. The text is yours. It was written for exactly this moment. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating, today as always. When you finish them, you will have finished Computing Foundations. I am Professor Ye-Jin Kim, and it has been my pleasure to teach a student who does the work. Settle your notes, take a breath, and begin. When the last question is answered, close the book gently. The machine in your pocket will still be there, counting, fetching, keeping, and talking, exactly as it was this morning. The difference is in you, and the difference is permanent, and it is yours.
